stem: A security administrator at an electric cooperative exports the control register below.
ask: Which of the following control categories applies to CTRL-07?

lines: CTRL-07  Acceptable use document signed by each new hire
CTRL-12  Badge reader on the data hall door
CTRL-19  Endpoint agent blocks unsigned programs
CTRL-23  Help desk calls the user back before a reset

why: That fits CTRL-19, where the endpoint agent enforces the rule; CTRL-07 is a document.
An acceptable use document is a policy that guides behavior, which is managerial.
That fits CTRL-12, the badge reader on a door; CTRL-07 protects no space.
That fits CTRL-23, a task the help desk performs; CTRL-07 is a policy.

stem: A new security analyst at a ferry company drafts notes on the control categories for a team briefing.
ask: Which of the following notes are accurate? (Select TWO)
options: Operational means people carry the control out
Physical means a system enforces the rule
A category names the goal a control serves
why: Operational controls are performed by people in daily work.
A system enforcing a rule is technical; physical controls protect spaces and assets.
Administrative is the other name for the managerial category.
Written policies are managerial; technical controls are enforced by hardware, software or firmware.
The goal is the control type; the category is how the control is implemented.

source.chapter: Technical vs managerial vs operational vs physical controls (control categories compared)

ask: Which of the following describes an operational control?
options: A system enforces it with no person
Leadership decides it in a policy
People perform it in daily work
A barrier protects a room or site
why: That describes a technical control.
That describes a managerial control.
Operational controls are carried out by people as part of daily operations.
That describes a physical control.

ask: Which of the following controls is operational?
options: Locks on the server room doors
why: Antivirus is software enforcing rules by itself, which is technical.
A written policy is managerial.
Training is delivered and followed by people, which makes it operational.
Locks protect a space, which is physical.

stem: At a call center, a supervisor walks the floor at the end of each shift and checks that no customer printouts are left on desks.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes the supervisor's check?
why: Nothing tangible blocks access here; a person performs the check.
A rule about printouts would be managerial, but the walk is the work itself.
No system enforces the check.
A person performing a routine check during daily operations is operational.

stem: At a pharmaceutical warehouse, the receptionists compare each visitor's photo ID with the expected visitor list by hand and phone the visitor's host before signing the visitor in.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes the receptionists' checks?
why: Nothing tangible blocks entry or watches an area; the control is the checking work the receptionists do.
The receptionists perform the ID check and the call by hand as part of their daily work.
No system makes the decision; the receptionists compare IDs and phone hosts themselves.
No policy or risk decision is described; this is a task performed at the desk.

stem: Each morning, an analyst at an online retailer reads the previous night's login records and flags anything unusual to her manager.
ask: Which of the following control categories does the morning review belong to?
why: A person reviewing records as part of daily work is operational.
The records come from systems, but a person reads and judges them.
No policy or risk decision is described; this is routine work.
Nothing protects a space or a device.

stem: When an employee at a staffing agency asks for access to the finance share, an administrator phones the employee's manager to confirm the request before granting it.
ask: Which of the following explains why the phone confirmation is an operational control?
options: A person performs the check by hand
A written rule makes the check happen
why: The administrator makes the call as part of daily work, which is what makes it operational.
No system decides anything; the administrator chooses to call and judges the answer.
A rule requiring confirmation would be managerial, but the stem describes the call itself.
The call protects access to a file share, not a room or building.

stem: A trainer at a city council runs hands-on sessions in which staff practice spotting and reporting suspicious emails.
ask: Which of the following control categories BEST describes the sessions?
why: Deciding to require training is managerial, but the stem describes sessions being delivered.
No system enforces anything; a trainer and staff do the work.
Delivering training to staff is security work people carry out, which is operational.
Nothing protects a space or equipment.

stem: Each morning, the night operator at an insurance broker reads the backup report and reruns by hand any backup job that failed overnight.
ask: Which of the following explains why this task is an operational control?
options: A system carries it out with no person
A person does it as routine work
A written policy makes it happen
A barrier guards a room or building
why: The backup software runs the jobs, but the control asked about is the operator reading the report and rerunning failures.
The operator does the check and the rerun by hand every morning, which is operational.
No policy or risk decision is described; the stem describes daily work.
The task protects no space or equipment from physical access.

stem: A system administrator at a seaport keeps the shift checklist below.
ask: Which of the following control categories describes the 07:00 entry?

lines: 06:15  Server room door checked and found locked
07:00  Yesterday's firewall rule changes compared by hand with approved tickets, 1 change queried

why: The firewall itself is technical, but the 07:00 entry is a comparison the administrator makes by hand.
The 06:15 entry concerns a door; the 07:00 entry concerns firewall changes and tickets.
Approving changes is not what the entry records; it records a routine comparison on the shift.
A person checks each change against its ticket as part of the shift's routine, which is operational.

stem: The manager of a distribution center must add two controls in the operational category before the next audit.
ask: Which of the following meet this requirement? (Select TWO)
options: Shift leads counting scanners back in nightly
A badge reader on the warehouse door
An acceptable use policy for handheld scanners
Supervisors reviewing camera footage each shift
why: Shift leads counting the scanners back in is a routine task people do, which is operational.
A badge reader on a door is a physical control.
A policy is a managerial control.
People reviewing footage on a schedule is operational work.
The system locks the account by itself, which is technical.

ask: Which of the following describes a deterrent control?
options: It blocks an attempt before it starts
It discourages but does not stop
It identifies an event and raises an alert
It repairs systems after an incident
why: That describes a preventive control.
A deterrent works on the attacker's choice and does not block the attempt.
That describes a detective control.
That describes a corrective control.

ask: Which of the following controls is a deterrent?
options: A login banner warning of prosecution
A firewall rule blocking inbound traffic
why: A warning of prosecution discourages misuse but does not block a login.
Blocking traffic is preventive.
An alert identifies an event, which is detective.
Restoring after an event is corrective.

stem: The IT director at a software company adds a notice to every staff login screen saying that misuse can lead to dismissal. Staff can still sign in and use the system as normal.
ask: Which of the following control types does the notice serve?
why: The notice warns of a consequence to discourage misuse without blocking anyone.
The notice blocks nothing; staff still sign in as normal.
The notice itself records nothing and raises no alert.
Nothing has happened that needs repair.

stem: The office manager at an architecture firm places a uniformed guard at the reception desk. The manager says the main reason is so that people with bad intentions decide not to try entering.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the stated reason for the guard?
why: A guard can also block entry, but the stated reason is to make people decide not to try.
The guard is not standing in for another control that the firm cannot use.
Making people decide not to try is discouraging the attempt, which is deterrence.
Nothing is being repaired after an event.

stem: A trading firm's handbook states that sharing a trading password will lead to demotion. Nothing in the trading systems stops a trader from sharing one.
ask: Which of the following control types does the threat of demotion serve?
why: Nothing stops a trader from sharing, so nothing is prevented.
The threat of demotion discourages sharing without stopping it.
The threat does not identify or record any sharing.
Nothing is repaired; the threat acts before any sharing.

stem: A technician arriving at a data center sees a sign on the door that reads: 'Unauthorized entry will be reported to the police.'
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the sign?
why: A sign telling people what to do would be directive, but this one warns of what happens.
The sign does not stop anyone opening the door.
The sign records nothing and raises no alert.
The sign warns of a consequence, which discourages entry.

stem: The HR director at a payroll company announces in the staff newsletter that an employee was dismissed for copying customer files to a personal drive. The aim is that others with the same idea decide not to try. Nothing about file access changes.
ask: Which of the following control types does the announcement serve?
why: The announcement finds no copying; it reports a case already handled.
Nothing about file access changes, so no copy is blocked.
It gives no instruction on how to handle files; it shows what happened to someone who broke the rule.
Showing the consequence works only on the decision to try, which is deterrence.

stem: The IT manager at a health clinic protects its remote admin portal only with a warning banner. An attacker who ignores the warning signs in with a stolen password.
ask: Which of the following control types would have stopped the sign-in?
why: The banner is already deterrent, and the attacker ignored it.
A preventive control blocks the action, which a warning cannot do.
Detection could notice the sign-in afterward but would not stop it.
Instructions rely on compliance, which this attacker ignores.

stem: When a records clerk at a county office opens a remote session to the records server, the session begins with the screen below.
ask: Which of the following control types does this screen provide?

lines: NOTICE: All sessions on this server are logged.
Misuse will be referred for prosecution.

why: The screen warns of prosecution to discourage misuse.
Pressing Enter lets anyone continue, so nothing is blocked.
The logging behind the screen is detective, but the screen itself only warns.
Nothing is being repaired after an event.

stem: The owner of a self-storage business wants controls that discourage break-ins without blocking or recording anything.
ask: Which of the following meet this requirement? (Select TWO)
options: Signs warning that the site is monitored
Bright lights over the storage rows
An alarm log reviewed each morning
Replacing broken locks after a theft
why: Warning signs discourage an attempt without stopping it.
Bright lighting makes thieves feel seen, which discourages them.
Padlocks block entry, which is preventive.
Reviewing an alarm log identifies events, which is detective.
Repairing after a theft is corrective.

ask: Which of the following describes a preventive control?
options: It discourages an attempt without stopping it
It blocks an incident before it happens
It records an event so it can be investigated
It restores systems after an event
why: That describes a deterrent control.
Preventive controls stop the event before it occurs by restricting access or actions.
That describes a detective control.
That describes a corrective control.

ask: Which of the following controls is preventive?
options: A banner warning that misuse is prosecuted
why: Locking the account blocks further guessing.
A warning banner discourages but does not block, which is deterrent.
Log review identifies events after they happen, which is detective.
Restoring after an event is corrective.

stem: The operations manager at a bakery chain fits the stockroom with a door that stays locked until an employee enters the right code, so no one else can walk in.
ask: Which of the following control types does the coded lock provide?
why: The lock does not rely on anyone choosing to stay out; it keeps them out.
The lock does not record or alert; it blocks.
The lock blocks entry for anyone without the code.
Nothing has happened yet that needs repair.

stem: The IT contractor at a dental practice has set the firewall to drop every inbound connection from the internet to its patient database server before the connection reaches the server.
ask: Which of the following control types does the firewall provide here?
why: Dropping the connection stops it rather than only reporting it.
Dropping the connection before it arrives blocks it.
Nothing depends on the sender choosing to stop; the connection is refused.
Nothing is being repaired after an event.

stem: A university's network engineer places a sensor in line with campus traffic. The sensor drops any packet that matches a known attack pattern.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the sensor?
why: The sensor drops the matching packets, which blocks the attack.
The sensor does identify attack patterns, but it also drops the packets, which goes past detection.
Nothing here relies on discouraging the attacker.
The sensor acts before the packet arrives, not after damage.

stem: The IT administrator at a veterinary clinic sets the booking system to lock any account after five wrong passwords in a row. No one has tried to guess a password yet.
ask: Which of the following control types does this setting provide?
why: Nothing has gone wrong yet; corrective controls act after an event to restore normal operation.
The lockout stops further guesses rather than only recording them.
The lockout is a standard safeguard in its own right, not a substitute for one that cannot be used.
Locking the account stops a password-guessing attempt before it can succeed.

stem: The office manager at a law office turns on full-disk encryption on its laptops so that the files on a stolen laptop cannot be read.
ask: Which of the following control types does the encryption provide?
why: Encryption does not record or report a theft.
Encryption is in place before any theft; corrective acts after.
Encryption prevents unauthorized reading of the files.
Encryption does not depend on discouraging a thief; it keeps the files unreadable.

stem: The desktop administrator at a payroll firm configures the workstations so that only programs on an approved list can start. Any other program is refused.
ask: Which of the following control types does this configuration provide?
why: A list of approved programs in a handbook would be directive; here the workstation refuses the rest.
The configuration blocks programs rather than only reporting them.
Programs not on the list are refused, so they never run.
Nothing here substitutes for a control that cannot be used.

stem: An administrator at a seafood exporter applies the rules below to the mail server's network interface.
ask: Which of the following control types does the second rule provide?

lines: access-list 110 permit tcp any host 192.0.2.25 eq 25

why: The rule does not alert; it refuses the traffic.
No one is shown a warning; the traffic is simply blocked.
Nothing has gone wrong that needs repair.
The rule refuses all other traffic to the server before it arrives.

stem: A warehouse manager wants controls that actually stop an intruder getting in, rather than ones that only discourage or record an attempt.
ask: Which of the following meet this requirement? (Select TWO)
options: A No Entry sign on the fence
A locked gate at the loading bay
An access control vestibule at the entrance
why: A sign only instructs or discourages; it stops no one.
A camera records the attempt; it does not stop it.
Lighting discourages but does not block entry.
A locked gate blocks entry.
A vestibule holds a person until they are cleared, which blocks entry.

ask: Which of the following describes a compensating control?
options: A stand-in for a measure that cannot be used
A repair made after an incident has happened
A barrier that stops an event before it starts
An instruction telling people what to do
why: A compensating control gives similar protection when the required control cannot be put in place.
That describes a corrective control.
That describes a preventive control.
That describes a directive control.

ask: Which of the following situations calls for a compensating control?
options: An attack has already caused damage
An attacker should be discouraged from trying
An event must be spotted as it happens
A required safeguard cannot be put in place
why: Repairing damage after an attack calls for a corrective control.
Discouraging attempts calls for a deterrent control.
Spotting events calls for a detective control.
Compensating controls exist for exactly this case.

stem: A city's traffic signal controller runs firmware that cannot accept security updates. Until the controller is replaced, the city's traffic engineer places it behind a firewall that admits connections from just two engineering laptops.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the firewall arrangement?
why: The firewall does block traffic, but it is there because the updates cannot be applied.
No incident has happened; nothing is being repaired.
The firewall stands in for the security updates the controller cannot accept.
The firewall enforces access; it does not just tell people what to do.

stem: A two-person accounting office cannot split payment duties between different people. To make up for this, the owner reviews every payment record at the end of each day.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the owner's daily review?
why: Reviewing records is detective work, but it is done because the duties cannot be split.
No incident has happened; nothing is being repaired.
The review stands in for the separation of duties the office cannot have.
The review does not tell anyone what to do.

stem: A factory's milling machine runs software that cannot run antivirus. Until the machine is replaced, the plant manager keeps it off the network and loads files onto it only from one checked USB drive.
ask: Which of the following control types does the plant's arrangement provide?
why: No incident has happened; nothing is being repaired.
The arrangement is enforced, not just an instruction to staff.
Nothing here aims to discourage an attacker.
Keeping the machine off the network stands in for the antivirus it cannot run.

stem: A water utility's standard requires multifactor sign-in, but its old billing application cannot support it. The utility's IT manager now has users reach the application only through a gateway server that does require multifactor sign-in.
ask: Which of the following describes the role the gateway plays here?
options: It repairs the software after a breach
It stands in for a feature the app lacks
It records each sign-in for later review
It tells staff how to sign in safely
why: Nothing was breached; repairing after an event would be corrective.
The gateway gives the multifactor protection the application itself cannot provide, which is compensating.
The gateway enforces a second factor; it does not only record sign-ins.
Users are not just told what to do; the gateway enforces the second factor.

stem: A facilities manager at a translation agency must add badge readers to every server room door under the company's security standard. The lease of the office building forbids any wiring through the doors, so under an approved exception the manager instead keeps the servers in locked cabinets whose keys sit in a logged key safe.
ask: Which of the following control types do the locked cabinets provide in this case?
why: No incident has happened; nothing is being repaired.
The cabinets stand in for the badge readers the lease does not allow, guarding the same servers.
The cabinets physically keep people out; they are not instructions to staff.
The cabinets are not there to discourage anyone; they replace the required readers.

stem: A jeweler's insurer requires that any after-hours entry to the stock room be detected and answered within minutes, and recommends a night guard, which the shop cannot afford. With the insurer's written approval, the store manager instead installs a door alarm monitored by a firm that sends a responder within minutes.
ask: Which of the following control types BEST describes the alarm in this case?
why: The alarm meets the same requirement the guard would have met, in place of a guard the shop cannot afford.
The alarm detects entry, but it was put in place instead of the guard the insurer recommended and meets the same requirement.
No incident has happened; nothing is being repaired.
The alarm does not tell anyone what to do.

stem: An auditor at a museum reads the exception record below.
ask: Which of the following describes the in_place_instead line?

lines: required: full-disk encryption on all devices
in_place_instead: no visitor data stored locally, kiosk bolted to the wall

options: A repair made after an earlier incident
A substitute for a missing safeguard
why: No incident is recorded; nothing is being repaired.
The line lists measures in place, not instructions to staff.
The line lists what stands in for the encryption the kiosk cannot support, which is compensating.
Nothing in the line identifies or records events.

stem: A risk analyst at a logistics firm reviews a colleague's summary of compensating controls.
ask: Which of the following statements in the summary are accurate? (Select TWO)
options: It is applied after an incident to restore systems
It addresses the same risk as the missing control
It is any cheaper control chosen to save money
It is often temporary until the ideal control is possible
It only tells staff what they should do
why: Restoring after an incident is corrective.
A compensating control must give similar protection against the same risk.
It must address the same risk to a comparable degree; cost alone does not make one.
It is often a stand-in until the system can take the ideal control.
Telling staff what to do is directive.

ask: Which of the following AAA functions decides what a user who has proven an identity may do?
why: Authentication proves who the user is; it does not decide their rights.
Accounting records what the user did; it does not decide what is allowed.
Identification is only the claim of an identity, such as typing a username.
Authorization decides what an authenticated user is allowed to do.

ask: Which of the following gives the order of the AAA steps after a user claims an identity?
why: Rights cannot be decided for an identity that has not been proven yet.
The identity is proven first, then rights are decided, then activity is recorded.
Accounting records what was done, so it cannot come before access is granted.
Rights are decided before the session is recorded, so accounting comes last.

stem: A network administrator at a city transit agency needs a record of when each VPN session started and stopped and how much data it moved.
ask: Which of the following AAA functions provides this record?
why: Authorization decides what the user may reach; it does not record the session.
Accounting logs session start, stop and data use.
Authentication proves who connected; it does not track the session afterward.
Identification is the username claim; it records nothing.

stem: A visiting researcher at a university logs in successfully with her username and password, but her request to open the grants database is refused.
ask: Which of the following AAA functions refused the request?
why: Authentication succeeded; the stem says she logged in successfully.
Accounting records activity; it does not grant or refuse requests.
Identification is only the username claim, which was already accepted.
She proved her identity, but authorization decided she may not open that database.

stem: An incident responder at a seed distributor finds that a temporary account signed in to the file server and was allowed into the finance share last week. Nothing on any system shows which files the account opened or how long it stayed.
ask: Which of the following AAA functions was not working for this account?
why: The account signed in, so its sign-in was checked; authentication did its job.
The account was allowed into the finance share, so a decision about its access was made.
Accounting records what an account did, such as resources used and time spent, and no such record exists.
The account name was claimed at sign-in; the missing piece is a record of activity afterward.

stem: A help desk technician at a dental group explains that the name a user types first proves nothing by itself, and the user must then show something that backs the claim.
ask: Which of the following steps does entering that name alone accomplish?
why: Authentication is the next step, when the user backs the claim with a factor.
Authorization decides rights after the identity is proven.
Typing a username is the claim of an identity, which is identification.
Accounting records activity during the session.

stem: A systems administrator at a call center wants one central server to check VPN logins, place each user in an access group, and log each session for every remote office.
ask: Which of the following would provide all three functions?
why: A certificate authority issues certificates; it does not assign groups or log sessions.
A syslog server stores logs, but it does not check logins or assign access.
A web proxy relays web traffic; it does not authenticate VPN users or assign access groups.
A RADIUS server handles authentication, authorization and accounting for network access.

stem: A network manager at a telecom configures TACACS+ so that every command an engineer types on a core switch is checked against the engineer's permitted command list before it runs.
ask: Which of the following AAA functions performs the per-command check?
why: Authentication happened once at login; it does not judge each command.
Deciding whether each command is allowed is authorization.
Accounting records the commands after they run; it does not allow or refuse them.
Identification is the username claim at the start of the session.

stem: A network administrator at a freight railroad reads the AAA server records below.
ask: Which of the following AAA functions decided the outcome on the first line?
why: Authorization decided lines 2 and 3, where commands were permitted or denied.
Accounting wrote these records, but it did not decide to accept the login.
Accepting the login means the user's proof of identity was verified, which is authentication.
Identification is only the username claim; accepting the login required proof.

ask: Which of the following are examples of accounting? (Select TWO)
options: Checking a password against a stored hash
Placing a user in a group allowed to reach a share
Logging session start and stop times
Recording how much data a user moved
Typing a username at the login screen
why: Verifying a password proves identity, which is authentication.
Granting access through a group is authorization.
Recording when sessions began and ended is accounting.
Tracking resources used is accounting.
Claiming an identity is identification.

ask: Which of the following does the term video surveillance refer to?
options: Guards who patrol and answer alarms
Cameras that watch and record an area
Cards that unlock doors and log entries
A barrier that marks a site's boundary
why: That describes security guards, people rather than cameras.
Video surveillance is cameras (CCTV) that monitor and record what happens.
That describes access badges.
That describes fencing.

ask: Which of the following is the main job of a camera system in physical security?
options: Physically blocking entry to an area
Stopping vehicles at a building front
why: A camera blocks no one; barriers such as fences and doors do.
Holding people between doors is an access control vestibule.
Stopping vehicles is the job of bollards.
Cameras are mainly detective: they show events live and keep a record.

stem: The manager of a public swimming pool keeps 30 days of camera recordings. A new desk clerk asks why the recordings are kept at all, since the cameras cannot stop anyone from walking in.
ask: Which of the following explains why the recordings are kept?
options: To bar entry to the changing rooms
To review events after an incident
To undo the damage after a theft
To mark where the pool grounds end
why: The stem says the cameras cannot stop anyone; barring entry is the job of a barrier.
Kept recordings let staff see later who was where, and they serve as evidence in an investigation.
Footage restores nothing; it only shows what happened.
Marking a boundary is the job of a fence, not of a recording.

stem: The night manager of a self-storage site wants an alert on his phone whenever anyone moves through the empty corridors. He also wants a clip of each event saved for later.
ask: Which of the following should the manager install?
why: Posts stop vehicles; they send no alerts and record nothing.
A fence slows entry but neither alerts on movement nor records it.
Cameras with motion detection send an alert when someone appears and keep the footage.
A booth controls entry at a door; it does not watch the corridors.

stem: The property manager of an apartment complex wants a list of the plates of every car that enters the residents' gated lot.
ask: Which of the following provides this list?
options: Steel posts at the lot entry
A fence around the whole lot
why: Posts can keep cars out but cannot read or list plates.
A badge log lists badges used, not the plates of the cars that came in.
A fence keeps people out but records nothing about cars.
Modern cameras can read license plates and record them.

stem: The loss prevention manager of a home goods chain wants to identify shoplifters after the fact and hand the police recorded evidence of each theft.
ask: Which of the following controls BEST meets this goal?
why: A guard may witness a theft, but a witness is not a recording that can be handed over.
Shoppers carry no badges, so badge logs say nothing about them.
Recordings show who took what and can be handed to the police.
A pressure sensor reports weight at one spot and identifies no one.

stem: The operations lead at an airport cargo terminal wants the camera system to flag any bag that is left on the floor unattended for more than 10 minutes.
ask: Which camera feature provides this?
why: Motion detection reacts to movement; a bag lying still does not move.
Object detection recognizes items in view, such as a bag left behind.
Facial recognition identifies people by their faces, not bags.
Plate reading identifies vehicles, not items on the floor.

stem: A security analyst at a fuel distributor exports the event list below from the night of a theft at a depot.
ask: Which control produced these events?
why: A camera that detects motion, recognizes a person and stores a clip is video surveillance.
An infrared sensor detects body heat but cannot recognize a person or store a clip.
A pressure sensor reports weight at one spot and stores no images.
A microwave sensor detects movement but records no picture.

stem: The facilities director of a school district wants footage from cameras at 14 schools kept in one place, so that investigators at the district office can search all of it.
ask: Which of the following meets this need?
options: Sending all footage to central storage
Keeping footage on each camera's own card
Posting a guard at every school entrance
Issuing badges to every school visitor
why: Modern systems send footage from many cameras to central storage, where it can be searched.
Footage left on each camera stays at 14 separate schools.
Guards watch entrances but do not gather footage into one place.
Badges control doors; they do not collect camera footage.

stem: The operations manager of a gym chain mounts cameras in clear view above each front desk, recording around the clock.
ask: Which of the following control types do these cameras provide? (Select TWO)
why: Cameras record events so they can be seen and investigated.
Cameras in clear view discourage wrongdoing by people who see them.
A camera blocks nothing; anyone can still reach the desk.
Cameras restore nothing after an incident.
Nothing in the stem says the cameras stand in for a control that could not be used.

ask: Which of the following describes an implicit trust zone?
options: The area behind a PEP, trusted after passing it
The whole internal network, trusted by default
The plane where access decisions are made
why: Entities are trusted once they have passed through the enforcement point in front of the zone.
Zero Trust specifically avoids treating the whole internal network as trusted.
Decisions are made in the control plane, not in a trust zone.
The requester sits outside, on the untrusted side of the gateway.

ask: What size should implicit trust zones be under Zero Trust?
options: As large as the internal network
why: A network-wide zone is the flat design Zero Trust avoids.
Size is set by resources behind each enforcement point, not by buildings.
Small zones limit what anything inside can reach without another check.
A department-wide zone is still large; Zero Trust keeps each zone as small as possible.

stem: After the gateway at a credit union branch admits a teller's session, traffic between that gateway and the core banking server is not checked again.
ask: Which of the following describes the segment between the gateway and the server?
why: The control plane is where decisions are made, not the path behind the gateway.
The teller and device are the requester, before the gateway.
The Policy Engine is a decision component, not a network segment.
Traffic past the gateway is trusted without further checks, which is an implicit trust zone.

stem: A network engineer at a manufacturing plant finds that once any device passes the main gateway, it can reach every server in the plant.
ask: Which of the following does Zero Trust say about this design?
options: It is the ideal Zero Trust layout
It is a large trust zone to shrink
It is a control plane to protect
why: Zero Trust wants small zones, not one large one.
A flat network behind one gateway is a large implicit trust zone, which Zero Trust avoids.
The servers behind the gateway are not the decision-making plane.
Zero Trust adds enforcement points closer to resources, not fewer.

stem: A security architect at a data center provider must fix a design in which one gateway admits workstations to a segment holding 40 servers, in line with Zero Trust.
ask: Which of the following is the BEST change?
options: Add a stronger firewall at the segment edge
Place enforcement points in front of each server
Move the segment to a new address range
why: It strengthens the one gate, but all 40 servers stay in one large zone behind it.
Stronger passwords do nothing about what is reachable after the gateway.
Moving checks next to each server shrinks the zone from 40 servers to one.
Readdressing leaves the same single gateway and the same large zone.

stem: A trainer at an airline explains the comparison NIST uses for implicit trust zones.
ask: Which of the following matches that comparison?
options: Passengers past the checkpoint are treated as trusted
Every passenger is searched again at each gate
Passengers outside the airport are trusted
Only the crew may pass the checkpoint
why: Once through airport security, everyone in the boarding area is treated as trusted.
That would be continuous checking, not an implicit trust zone.
Trust comes after the checkpoint, not before it.
The comparison is about trust after the check, not who may enter.

stem: A junior administrator at a county hospital calls the screened subnet that hosts the public website an implicit trust zone.
ask: Which of the following is accurate?
options: They are two names for one thing
A screened subnet is the control plane
A screened subnet is where the PEP decides
why: A screened subnet is a network zone for public-facing servers; an implicit trust zone is the area behind a Zero Trust enforcement point.
They come from different ideas and are not the same.
A screened subnet is a network zone, not the Zero Trust decision plane.
The enforcement point never decides, and a screened subnet is not part of the Zero Trust planes.

stem: An incident responder at a weather service finds that malware on one forecasting server spread unchecked to the three other servers behind the same gateway. It reached no servers behind the service's other gateways.
ask: Which of the following describes the four servers behind that gateway?
why: Separate zones would each sit behind their own check, but the malware moved among the four unchecked.
The gateway in front of the servers is the enforcement point; the servers sit behind it.
Entities behind one enforcement point trust each other with no further checks, so the malware moved freely among the four.
The control plane decides and configures; it holds no application servers.

stem: A network architect at a biotech firm changes the enforcement layout below.
ask: Which of the following describes the effect of the change?
options: One trust zone now spans every server
Each trust zone now holds one service
The control plane now carries app traffic
Users no longer pass any enforcement point
why: That describes the before line, not the change.
Each enforcement point now guards a single service, so each zone behind it holds one.
The change moves enforcement points; the control plane still only decides.
Every app still has an enforcement point in front of it.

ask: Which of the following are accurate about implicit trust zones? (Select TWO)
options: The whole enterprise network should be one
They sit in the control plane
They lie behind a Policy Enforcement Point
Entities inside are checked at every hop
Zero Trust keeps them as small as possible
why: Zero Trust avoids treating the whole network as a trust zone.
They belong to the data plane.
The zone is the area trusted after passing the enforcement point.
Inside the zone, entities are trusted without further checks.
Small zones limit what passing one checkpoint grants.

ask: Which of the following describes the Zero Trust security model?
options: Users inside the network are trusted
No request is trusted by default, even inside
Trust is granted once a day at first login
Only traffic from the internet is checked
why: Trusting the inside is the old perimeter model that Zero Trust replaces.
Zero Trust authenticates, authorizes and checks every request, wherever it comes from.
Zero Trust checks each request; it does not hand out a day of trust.
Zero Trust checks internal requests as well; location grants no trust.

ask: Which of the following describes how a Zero Trust architecture is split?
options: Data plane decides, control plane enforces
Inside zone decides, outside zone enforces
Control plane decides and also enforces
Control plane decides, data plane enforces
why: This reverses the roles: deciding is the control plane's job.
Zero Trust does not split trust by inside and outside.
Enforcement happens in the data plane, where the traffic flows.
The control plane makes decisions; the data plane carries traffic and enforces them.

stem: A claims adjuster at an insurer works at the head office on the corporate network. Each time she opens the claims app, she must still sign in and pass a device health check.
ask: Which of the following explains why she is checked even on the corporate network?
options: The claims app sits outside the office
Head office devices are trusted by default
why: Nothing in the stem says the account is suspect; the checks happen every time.
Where the app is hosted does not change the rule; every request is checked.
Under Zero Trust, being inside the network does not earn trust, so every request is checked.
If they were trusted by default, she would not be checked.

stem: A pharmacist at a hospital opens the dispensing app from a ward workstation, and the request is checked against her identity and the workstation's state before access is granted, every time.
ask: Which of the following principles does this reflect?
why: Every request is verified, with no trust carried over from earlier requests or from location.
The stem says the check happens every time, not once.
The workstation is inside the building and is still checked.
She is on a ward workstation, not remote, and is still verified.

stem: A network manager at a game studio already requires the corporate VPN for remote staff. The manager now wants each request to each app checked for identity and device posture, wherever the user is.
ask: Which of the following describes the model the manager wants?
why: A perimeter model trusts users once they are inside, such as after joining the VPN.
A screened subnet is a network zone for public-facing servers, not a per-request check.
A VPN joins networks; it does not check each request to each app.
Checking every request for identity and device posture, regardless of location, is Zero Trust.

stem: At a trade show, a vendor tells an IT director at a credit union that buying one appliance will make the network Zero Trust.
ask: Which of the following is accurate about the vendor's claim?
options: Zero Trust requires that one appliance
Zero Trust is a model, not one product
Zero Trust removes the need for firewalls
Zero Trust means never trusting any user
why: No specific product is required; it is a model.
Zero Trust is a set of principles and an architecture; no single box delivers it.
Firewalls and segmentation stay; they stop being the only gate.
Trust is earned per request, not refused forever.

stem: After an attacker stole a contractor's VPN password at an electric utility, the security team found the attacker could reach every internal system once connected.
ask: Which of the following was missing from the utility's design?
options: A gap analysis against a framework
why: Encryption at rest protects stored data but does not stop a connected user reaching systems.
Once connected, the attacker was trusted everywhere, which is implicit trust by location.
Accounting records sessions; it would not have limited what the attacker reached.
A gap analysis plans improvements; it does not check each request.

stem: A cloud architect at a biotech firm explains to new staff that the firm's Zero Trust design still uses firewalls and network segmentation.
ask: Which of the following is accurate about firewalls under Zero Trust?
options: They are removed from the network
They make the inside fully trusted
They remain, but are not the only gate
why: Zero Trust does not require removing firewalls.
Zero Trust grants no trust for being inside.
Identity checks on every request are central to Zero Trust.
Zero Trust keeps firewalls and segmentation, but every request is also checked.

stem: A security analyst at a freight broker reviews an access decision for a user who is already on the office network.
ask: Which of the following explains the result?
options: The user failed the MFA prompt
The user was outside the network
why: posture=noncompliant shows the laptop failed the device check, so access was denied.
mfa=passed shows the user completed MFA.
The stem says the user is on the office network, and the log line shows the denial follows the failed posture check.
The line records a decision to deny, not an outage.

ask: Which of the following are core ideas of Zero Trust? (Select TWO)
options: Internal users are trusted after login
Every request is authenticated and authorized
Network location grants no implicit trust
A firewall alone protects internal systems
Devices are checked only once a year
why: That is the perimeter model; Zero Trust keeps checking.
Zero Trust checks every subject and every request.
Being inside the network earns nothing by itself.
Zero Trust adds per-request checks; the firewall is not the only gate.
Device posture is checked when access is requested.

ask: Which of the following describes a pressure sensor?
options: A sensor that detects changes in heat
A sensor that reads reflected radio pulses
A sensor that detects weight or force on a surface
A sensor that reads echoes of high-pitched sound
why: Heat is sensed by an infrared sensor.
Reflected radio pulses are how a microwave sensor works.
A pressure sensor reacts to force or weight applied to a surface.
Sound echoes are how an ultrasonic sensor works.

ask: Which of the following is a typical place for a pressure sensor?
options: High in the corner of a room
On a pole watching the parking lot
Along the top of the boundary fence
why: A corner mount suits a motion detector that watches a room, not a weight sensor.
Pressure sensors sit in floor mats and pressure-sensitive surfaces where people step.
A pole above a lot is a place for a camera.
The top of a fence holds wire or topping, not floor sensors.

stem: A records manager at a title insurance company wants an alert when anyone steps just inside the file room door. Tall shelving blocks any clear view of that spot from the walls and ceiling.
ask: Which of the following sensors fits this spot?
why: A pressure sensor reacts to weight and does not need a line of sight.
An infrared sensor must see the area, and the shelving blocks its view.
A camera must see the spot, and the shelving blocks it.
Lighting helps people see but raises no alert by itself.

stem: A security coordinator at a stock brokerage wants an alarm only when someone steps onto the landing at the top of the stairs to the executive floor. Movement anywhere else on that floor must not trigger it.
ask: Which of the following sensors fits this need?
why: A mat on the landing reports weight at that exact spot only.
Microwave covers a large area and would react to movement elsewhere on the floor.
Ultrasonic fills a room with sound and reacts to movement anywhere in it.
Infrared watches zones across an area, not one exact step.

stem: An alarm installer puts a sensor under the mat at the back door of a bakery. The ovens keep the room hot, and the room is dark at night.
ask: Which of the following explains why a pressure sensor suits this spot?
options: It reacts to the heat of the ovens
It reacts to weight, not to heat or light
It records whoever steps on the mat
It stops anyone opening the back door
why: Reacting to heat would cause false alarms here; that is an infrared sensor's weakness, not this one's.
Heat from the ovens and darkness do not affect a sensor that reacts only to weight.
A pressure sensor records no images; a camera would.
A sensor stops no one; it reports.

stem: After a dental lab rearranged its office, the office manager finds that the alarm at the entry hall triggers constantly whenever the system is armed. A heavy filing cabinet now stands just inside the entry hall.
ask: Which of the following explains the constant alarms?
options: The cabinet blocks an infrared sensor's view
The cabinet reflects the microwave signal
The cabinet is pressing on a floor mat
The cabinet changes the hall's sound echoes
why: A blocked view makes an infrared sensor miss people, not alarm constantly.
A cabinet that stands still does not change the reflections, so it causes no motion alarm.
A heavy object resting on a pressure mat keeps its circuit triggered.
Echoes from an object that stands still do not change, so an ultrasonic sensor stays quiet.

stem: During a test at a gold refinery, a penetration tester steps over the floor mat at the vault door. The mat shows as a raised bump in the carpet.
ask: Which of the following would fix the weakness the tester found?
options: Raise the weight needed to trigger it
Move the mat into plain view
Turn the mat off during the day
Conceal the mat so no bump shows
why: A higher threshold makes the mat less sensitive, and the tester still sees and avoids it.
A mat in plain view is even easier to step over.
Daytime settings do not change how easily it is seen and avoided.
A mat works only if intruders do not know where it is; hidden, it cannot be stepped over on purpose.

stem: An operator at an alarm monitoring center sees the entries below for a client's cash office.
ask: Which of the following does the first entry report?

lines: 03:12:07  zone 12  floor mat  TAMPER  circuit open

options: The mat sensed body heat in the doorway
The mat's wiring was cut or disconnected
The mat sensed the door swinging open
why: A step is a normal alarm on the mat, not a tamper entry.
Mats sense weight, never heat.
A tamper entry with an open circuit means the cable was cut or unplugged.
A door opening is reported by a door contact, not a floor mat.

stem: The floor mat at the safe of a watch repair workshop triggered at 1 a.m., but the owner has no way to tell who stepped on it.
ask: Which control should the owner add to identify the person next time?
why: A camera records who was at the safe, which a mat cannot do.
Another sensor would also report presence but would not show who it was.
An ultrasonic sensor detects movement but identifies no one.
Light helps people and cameras see, but on its own it records no one.

stem: The manager of a ski resort's rental shop has pressure mats installed inside the doorway of the equipment store.
ask: Which of the following statements about the mats are accurate? (Select TWO)
options: They identify who stepped on them
They must stay in plain view to work
They report weight at one exact spot
They sense movement through the glass door
why: A mat reports a step, not the person; a camera identifies.
Mats work best hidden; in plain view they are stepped over.
A mat covers only the spot where it lies.
Sensing weight needs no light and no line of sight.
Mats sense nothing at a distance; sensing through glass is a microwave trait.

ask: Which of the following describes the Zero Trust data plane?
options: Where the access rules are written and stored
Where traffic flows and decisions are enforced
Where sign-in risk scores are worked out
why: Decisions are made in the control plane.
The rules are managed centrally and evaluated on the control plane side.
The data plane carries traffic and enforces what the control plane decided.
Risk evaluation is part of deciding, which is control plane work.

ask: Which of the following components belongs to the data plane?
why: The Policy Engine decides, in the control plane.
The enforcement point sits in the traffic path, on the data plane.
The Policy Administrator acts on decisions from the control plane.
Adaptive identity is a control plane concept for deciding.

stem: A traveling auditor's traffic at an accounting firm passes through a gateway, which lets the session through only because it was approved elsewhere.
ask: Which of the following parts of the architecture holds the gateway?
why: The approval came from the control plane; the gateway only enforces it.
The trust zone is the area behind the gateway, not the gateway itself.
The auditor and device are the subject/system making the request.
The gateway carries traffic and enforces an approval made elsewhere, which is data plane work.

stem: A Zero Trust designer at a hospital lists four parts of one request: the nurse, her tablet, the gateway and the zone behind the gateway.
ask: Which of the following parts of the architecture holds all four?
why: The control plane holds the decision makers, none of which are listed.
The Policy Engine is a single component that decides; it holds none of these.
Subject, system, enforcement point and implicit trust zone are all data plane parts.
The Policy Administrator is a single control plane component; it holds none of these.

stem: A security architect at a stock brokerage explains that attackers who reach the network carrying user traffic still cannot rewrite the access rules.
ask: Which of the following design choices makes this true?
options: The two planes are kept apart
The data plane makes all decisions
Every user shares one trust zone
The enforcement point stores the rules
why: Separating the control plane from the data plane keeps decision-making out of reach of user traffic.
If the data plane decided, reaching it would let attackers change decisions.
A large shared trust zone makes reach easier, not harder.
Putting rules in the traffic path would expose them to attackers there.

stem: A network engineer at a cartography firm labels each flow on the firm's Zero Trust diagram before a firewall review.
ask: Which of the following flows belongs on the data plane?
options: An instruction from the Policy Administrator to a gateway
A new access rule sent to the Policy Engine
A sign-in risk score sent to the Policy Engine
A map upload passing through a gateway to the app
why: The Policy Administrator instructs the gateway over the control plane.
Rules reach the decision maker over the control plane.
Risk scores feed the decision, which happens on the control plane.
Application traffic flows over the data plane, through the enforcement point.

stem: An engineer at a ride-sharing company traces a driver app's request to the trip database.
ask: Which of the following must the request pass through on the data plane before it reaches the database?
why: The Policy Engine decides on the control plane; traffic does not flow through it.
All traffic passes the enforcement point before reaching the resource.
The Policy Administrator instructs the gateway; traffic does not flow through it.
A gap analysis is a planning document, not part of the traffic path.

stem: A capacity planner at an online language school expects each student session to stream ten times more video next term. The number of sessions and the access rules will stay the same.
ask: Which of the following must be scaled up to carry the extra load?
why: The Policy Engine sits on the control plane and makes access decisions; no video passes through it, and the number of sessions stays the same.
Session traffic flows through the enforcement points on the data plane, so more video per session loads them.
The Policy Administrator sits on the control plane and sets up sessions, and their number does not change; the video never passes through it.
The rule store sits on the control plane; the access rules stay the same, and it carries no student traffic.

stem: A security architect at a home health agency drafts the component table below for a Zero Trust design.
ask: Which of the following belongs in place of the question mark?
why: The tablet makes requests; it does not decide them.
The tablet only requests access; it has no control plane role.
The subject/system is listed as part of the data plane.
The nurse's tablet is the system making requests, which sits on the data plane.

ask: Which of the following are found where traffic flows and decisions are enforced? (Select TWO)
options: The component that grants or denies
The requester and the device it uses
The component that issues session tokens
The zone trusted after the gateway
The logic that scores sign-in risk
why: That is the Policy Engine, in the control plane.
The subject/system is part of the data plane.
That is the Policy Administrator, in the control plane.
The implicit trust zone behind an enforcement point is part of the data plane.
Risk scoring is adaptive identity, a control plane concept.

ask: Which of the following describes deception and disruption technology?
options: Rules that block known attack traffic at the edge
Decoys that lure attackers and reveal their methods
Copies of real data kept for recovery after loss
Checks that prove who a user is before sign-in
why: Blocking known traffic is a filtering control, not a decoy.
Decoy systems and data draw attackers in, waste their time and show how they work.
Keeping copies for recovery is backup, which lures no one.
Proving identity is authentication, not deception.

Decoys block every attacker on contact
Decoys are placed only outside the network
Decoys have no legitimate users at all
why: Decoys hold fake data; nothing real is stored on them.
Decoys detect and divert; they do not block attackers.

Backing up the real file servers

stem: A trainee analyst at a gas utility writes flash cards for the four kinds of decoy. A mentor checks each one.

A honeyfile is one decoy file, not a network.
A honeytoken is a piece of traceable data, not a server.

stem: A board member at a marine insurer asks whether the new decoy servers will stop attacks on the real claims servers.

Yes, they encrypt the real servers' data
No, they detect and divert but block nothing

ask: Which of the following BEST meets this requirement?
why: An IDS detects intrusions too, but it judges ordinary traffic, so some alerts are false.
No normal traffic ever goes to a decoy, so its alerts are high confidence with few false positives.
Cameras watch physical spaces, not movement inside a network.

stem: A security analyst at a university reviews the alert below from the deception platform.
ask: Which of the following explains why the team should investigate 192.0.2.44 at once?

The decoy holds the HR team's real records
The login attempt on the decoy succeeded
The decoy blocked the host from the network

stem: A threat hunter at a toy maker lists this quarter's decoy alerts for the chief information security officer.
bullets: A sign-in attempt with a fake cloud key from an address outside the company
A scan of a fake file server from an office laptop
The opening of a fake salary spreadsheet on the HR share
Movement across three fake servers in the decoy network
ask: Which alert shows that a planted item was taken and then used outside the company?
why: The fake key was tried from outside the company, so it was copied out; tracing planted data like this is what a honeytoken does.
A scan of a decoy server shows probing inside the network; nothing was taken out.

ask: Which of the following statements in the runbook are accurate? (Select TWO)
options: Any contact with a decoy is suspicious
Decoys prevent attacks on real systems
Decoys must hold real data to work
Decoys need no isolation from production
why: No normal work touches a decoy.
Watching activity on decoys shows how attackers work.

Decoys hold fake data by design.
