ask: Which of the following describes a honeytoken?
options: A decoy file that alerts when it is opened
A single decoy system on the network
A set of linked decoy systems
Fake, traceable data with no legitimate use
why: A decoy file that alerts on access is a honeyfile.
A decoy system is a honeypot.
Linked decoy systems form a honeynet.
A honeytoken is a piece of fake data, such as a credential or address, whose use or sighting reveals a breach.

ask: Which of the following is a honeytoken designed to reveal?
options: That a decoy file was opened
That a decoy server was scanned
How an attacker moved between decoys
why: Reporting that a decoy file was opened is the job of a honeyfile.
Scans of a decoy server are reported by a honeypot.
A honeytoken is traceable, so its use or sighting shows where the data went.
Movement between decoys is shown by a honeynet.

stem: The privacy officer of an online florist adds a made-up email address to the customer mailing list. Only the florist's own systems ever send mail to it.
ask: Which of the following would show that the mailing list has leaked?
options: Staff opening the mailing list file at work
Outsiders sending mail to that inbox
A scan of the mail server from the internet
A drop in the number of subscribers
why: Staff open the real list as part of their jobs; that is normal use.
The address has no legitimate use outside, so mail from anyone else means the list got out.
Scans happen to any internet server and say nothing about the list leaking.
People unsubscribe for many reasons; it shows nothing about a leak.

stem: A systems administrator at a hospital chain creates a user account with a name like a real admin's. No one ever uses it, and any sign-in attempt with it raises an alert.
ask: Which of the following has the administrator created?
why: A fake credential with no legitimate use, watched for any attempt to use it, is a honeytoken.
A honeyfile is a decoy file that alerts when opened; this is an account.
A service account is a real account that a program uses for its work; this account is never used and exists only to raise an alert.
A honeynet is a network of decoy systems.

stem: A threat intelligence analyst at a card issuer plants a fake card number that looks valid but belongs to no customer. Weeks later the number appears in a list posted on a criminal forum.
ask: Which of the following does this sighting show?
options: Data from inside the company has leaked
An attacker opened a decoy file on a share
A decoy server was scanned from outside
A real customer's card was charged
why: The fake number existed only where it was planted, so its appearance shows that data left the issuer.
Nothing here is about a file being opened.
Nothing here is about a decoy server.
The number belongs to no customer, so no real card was involved.

stem: The risk officer of a payroll provider wants to learn whether its employee records are ever copied out. The theft might go unnoticed inside and come to light only when the data turns up somewhere else.
ask: Which of the following BEST meets this goal?
why: File integrity monitoring alerts when watched files change inside, not when copies turn up somewhere else.
Fake records planted among the real ones reveal the theft wherever they turn up.
A honeyfile alerts when that one decoy file is opened, not when copied employee records are used or seen elsewhere.
A honeynet shows movement between decoys, not where copied data goes.

stem: A database architect at an insurer mixes up tokenization and honeytokens in a design review.
ask: Which of the following describes the difference?
options: Honeytokens replace real card numbers to protect them
Tokenization plants decoys to catch attackers
Honeytokens are fake data planted to detect theft
why: Replacing real data with a stand-in to protect it is tokenization.
Tokenization protects real data; it plants no decoys.
A honeytoken is decoy data for detection; tokenization swaps real data for a stand-in to protect it.
Neither is encryption: one is a decoy, the other a substitution.

stem: An identity engineer at a software maker receives the alert below. The login named in it was planted in one place only.
ask: Which of the following does this alert show?

lines: planted only in: support bundle sent to vendor 2026-04-02

options: A decoy file on a share was opened
The VPN gateway itself was compromised
Vendor staff used the bundle's login for support
The vendor's copy of the bundle was exposed
why: No file was opened; a planted credential was used.
The gateway refused the login; the leak was of the credential, not the gateway.
A decoy login has no legitimate use, so no one should use it for support.
The decoy login lived only in the bundle sent to the vendor, so its use traces the leak there.

stem: During an incident review at a ticketing platform, the security engineer finds that an intruder tried a planted fake database password three weeks before anyone noticed. The password looked real and sat beside the real passwords in a deployment script.
ask: Which of the following was missing from this honeytoken?
options: An alert raised on any attempt
A place where real secrets are kept
Access to a real database account
why: A honeytoken detects only if its use is watched and reported at once; here the try went unnoticed for weeks.
The stem says the password looked real.
It sat beside the real passwords, where an intruder would look.
A honeytoken grants nothing real; it is fake data with no legitimate use.

stem: A deception planner at an online marketplace lists candidate decoys for the coming quarter.
ask: Which of the following candidates are honeytokens? (Select TWO)
options: A spreadsheet that alerts when opened
A fake API key placed in a config file
A made-up email address on the mailing list
A decoy server running a fake storefront
A network of fake storefront servers
why: A decoy file that alerts on access is a honeyfile.
A fake key is traceable data with no legitimate use.
A fake address is traceable data that reveals a leak when mail reaches it.
A decoy server is a honeypot.
A network of decoys is a honeynet.

ask: Which of the following describes security lighting?
options: Cameras that record activity during the night
Sensors that report body heat in the dark
Posts that keep cars off a walkway after dark
Light that deters intruders and helps cameras
why: That is video surveillance; lighting helps it but is a separate control.
That is an infrared sensor, which detects heat rather than lighting an area.
That is bollards, which stop vehicles at any hour.
Security lighting discourages intruders and helps cameras and guards see clearly.

ask: Which of the following lighting conditions makes camera footage harder to use?
options: Even light across the whole area
Lights aimed away from the cameras
Motion lights that switch on at doors
why: Even light is the goal: it removes shadows and helps cameras.
Aiming lights away from lenses avoids glare, which helps footage.
Shadows hide people and glare blinds the camera, so both ruin footage.
A light switching on at movement helps cameras capture the person.

stem: The security manager of a furniture maker reviews the cameras in its rear yard, which record clearly by day. At night the footage is too dark to identify anyone.
ask: Which of the following would fix the night footage?
options: Brighter, even lighting in the yard
More cameras of the same model in the yard
A taller fence around the yard
Badge readers on the yard gates
why: More even light lets the existing cameras capture usable images at night.
Cameras like the existing ones still record unusable images in the dark.
A taller fence slows intruders but does nothing for image quality.
Badge readers control the gates but do not light the yard.

stem: The owner of a marina wants would-be thieves walking along the docks at night to feel exposed and decide to leave.
ask: Which of the following controls fits this aim?
why: Bollards stop vehicles; people on foot walk past them unseen in the dark.
A vestibule controls a building door, not open docks.
An infrared sensor detects body heat quietly; an intruder does not feel exposed by it.
Bright light makes intruders feel seen, which discourages them.

stem: The security lead of a wildlife park must record the outer paddocks at night. Bright lights are not allowed there because they would disturb the animals.
ask: Which of the following meets this need?
why: The stem rules out bright lights in the paddocks.
Infrared cameras can work in low light, so the paddocks are recorded without bright lights.
A fence marks the boundary; it records nothing.
Badges control the gates; they record nothing inside the paddocks.

stem: A stone quarry's site manager has new floodlights pointed straight at the cameras in the equipment yard. Since then the night footage shows mostly white bloom.
ask: Which of the following explains why the footage got worse?
options: Light that is too even confuses cameras
Glare from the lights is blinding the cameras
Cameras cannot record under artificial light
Brighter areas make cameras switch off
why: Even light helps cameras; it is the aim of good lighting.
Light shining into a lens washes out the image; fixtures should be aimed at the area, not the cameras.
Cameras record well under artificial light that is aimed properly.
Cameras do not switch off in light; the problem is the light pointing into the lens.

stem: The caretaker of a church wants the side door lit only when someone comes near it, so that the light switching on draws attention to the person.
ask: Which of the following meets this need?
options: A light left on all night
An infrared sensor on the alarm
why: A light that is always on cannot draw attention by switching on.
A camera records and alerts, but it does not light the door.
An infrared sensor can trigger an alarm, but it gives no light.
It stays off until movement, and switching on draws attention to whoever approached.

stem: The facilities manager of a botanical garden reviews a lighting supplier's plan for the service yard behind the glasshouses, which three cameras watch at night.
ask: Which of the following weaknesses does this plan have?

lines: L1  floodlight on the gate post, aimed down at the gate
L2  floodlight over the loading door, aimed down at the door
Back wall (40 m): no fixtures, lit only by spill from L1 and L2
All fixtures aimed away from the camera lenses

options: Deep shadow along the back wall
Too little light at the gate
Too little light at the loading door
why: With no fixture of its own, the 40 m back wall stays dark, a place to hide and a stretch the cameras cannot see well.
The plan aims every fixture away from the lenses, so glare is avoided.
L1 is a floodlight aimed at the gate.
L2 is a floodlight aimed at the loading door.

stem: The night patrol supervisor of a nursing college has guards walk the path between the dorms and the library at night, and cameras record the same path. The guards cannot recognize anyone until they are a few steps away, and the footage shows only dark shapes.
ask: Which of the following would BEST help both the guards and the cameras?
options: A second guard on each patrol
why: Two guards in the dark still cannot recognize anyone, and the footage stays dark.
Infrared cameras can record in low light, but they do nothing for the guards on foot.
Mats report weight at one spot; they help neither the guards see nor the cameras record.
Light lets the guards recognize people and gives the cameras clear footage at the same time.

stem: The town manager of a seaside resort orders new lighting along the service lane behind its shops.
ask: Which of the following benefits does the new lighting bring? (Select TWO)
options: It physically blocks entry to the shops
It records who walks past at night
It stops vehicles reaching the shop fronts
It discourages people planning a break-in
why: Light blocks no one; barriers and locks do that.
Lights record nothing; cameras do.
Stopping vehicles is the job of bollards.
Intruders who feel seen are more likely to give up.
Better light means usable images at night.

ask: Which of the following describes an authorization model?
options: A key that encrypts stored files
Proof of identity with one or more factors
Rights mapped to users through roles or groups
A record of what each user did and when
why: Encryption protects confidentiality; it does not decide who may do what.
Proving identity is authentication, which happens before any model runs.
A model places an abstraction such as a role or group between users and permissions.
Recording activity is accounting.

ask: What is the main benefit of granting rights to roles instead of to individual users?
options: It removes the need to authenticate
It scales and is easier to audit
It logs every action users take
why: Users must still prove who they are before any rights apply.
One role grant covers many users, and reviewers can see who has what by role.
Roles organize permissions; they do not encrypt anything.
Logging actions is accounting, a separate function.

stem: A systems administrator at a food distributor must give every new warehouse picker the same access to the inventory app and two shared folders. Each picker's actions must stay traceable, and a later change to the pickers' access must reach all of them at once.
ask: Which of the following approaches meets these requirements?
options: Grant each picker rights to each resource
Give all pickers one shared account
Copy rights from a coworker for each picker
Grant rights to a picker role and add staff to it
why: Per-user grants must be changed for each picker one by one, so a later change does not reach all of them at once.
A shared account hides which picker did what, so actions are no longer traceable.
Copied rights are separate per-user grants, so a later change must be repeated for each picker.
Each picker keeps a personal account, and rights held by the role change once for every member.

stem: When a payroll specialist at an airline moves to the marketing team, an administrator removes her from one group, and every payroll right she had disappears at once.
ask: Which of the following explains why one change removed all of those rights?
options: Her rights were tied to her password
Her rights came through the group
Each of her rights was revoked separately
why: A password proves identity; it does not carry any rights.
Accounting records what she did; clearing them removes no rights.
Her payroll rights were granted to the group, so leaving it removed them all.
The stem says one change removed all of them, not many separate revocations.

stem: An identity engineer at a bus manufacturer assigns permissions to job functions such as welding supervisor and quality inspector, and each employee receives the permissions of the job held.
ask: Which of the following access control models is in use?
why: Permissions attached to job functions that staff receive by job is role-based access control.
In discretionary access control, resource owners grant access themselves, not by job function.
Mandatory access control uses labels and clearances, not job functions.
Rule-based access control applies system rules such as times or addresses, not job functions.

stem: A security analyst at a semiconductor fab finds that 1,200 users each hold rights granted one by one across 300 shares, and no one can say who has access to what.
ask: Which of the following changes addresses this problem?
options: Encrypt the contents of every share
why: MFA strengthens login but leaves the tangle of per-user rights in place.
Logs show what users did, not what they are allowed to do.
Encryption protects confidentiality; it does not organize who has access.
Moving rights onto roles makes access readable by role and easier to audit.

stem: A developer at an insurance startup proposes checking a caller's role before verifying the caller's login token, to save time on each request.
ask: Which of the following is the problem with this design?
options: Roles cannot be stored alongside login tokens
Rights cannot be decided for an unproven identity
Accounting must run before any check
Login tokens are a knowledge factor
why: Where roles are stored is not the issue; the order of the checks is.
Authorization must follow authentication; until the token is verified, the role claim may be false.
Accounting records the session after access is decided, not first.
Whether a token counts as a factor is not the issue; the problem is checking the role before the token is verified.

stem: An identity administrator at a theater company builds the Stage-Manager role as a directory group of that name, grants the role's rights to the group, and adds each stage manager to it.
ask: Which of the following is accurate about this setup?
options: Each member gets the role's rights one by one
The group carries the role's rights to its members
The group proves each member's identity
The group records what each member does
why: The rights go to the group, and members receive them through it, not one by one.
Many systems implement roles with groups: rights go to the group, and joining it grants the whole role.
A group decides what members may do; proving identity is authentication.
Recording activity is accounting; a group only carries rights.

stem: A systems administrator at a parcel service reviews the access setting below.
ask: Which of the following does lpatel still hold after being removed from the members line?
options: Read on manifests and write on labels
Read on rates, plus both role rights
No rights on fs02 at all
why: Those rights came only through the role, so removing the membership ends them.
The two role rights end with the membership; only the right granted to lpatel directly stays.
The rates right was granted to lpatel directly, so removing the membership leaves it in place.
The rates right was granted to lpatel directly, outside the role, so it survives the removal.

ask: Which of the following are benefits of assigning permissions through roles? (Select TWO)
options: Removes the need to authenticate users
Easier to audit who has what
Scales to many users and resources
why: Users must still prove their identity before rights apply.
Recording activity is accounting.
Reviewers can read access by role instead of by thousands of separate grants.
Roles exist to give each group only what its job needs.
One grant to a role covers every member.

ask: Which of the following describes a honeyfile?
options: Fake data that alerts when it is used elsewhere
One decoy system that draws attackers in
A network of linked decoy systems
A decoy file that raises an alert when accessed
why: Traceable data that alerts when used is a honeytoken.
A decoy system is a honeypot.
A network of decoys is a honeynet.
A honeyfile is a tempting fake file; any access to it triggers an alert.

ask: What sets off the alert of a honeyfile?
options: Someone logging in to a decoy server
Someone opening or copying the file
Someone stepping on a hidden floor mat
why: A login to a decoy server is a honeypot alert.
Movement between decoys is what a honeynet shows.
A honeyfile alerts on access, such as opening, copying or moving it.
A floor mat is a pressure sensor, a physical control.

stem: A security analyst at a cement maker places a file named "board-salaries-2027.xlsx" on the finance share. It holds made-up figures, and each time it is opened a message goes to security.
ask: Which of the following is this file?
why: A tempting file with fake contents that alerts when opened is a honeyfile.
A honeytoken alerts when a piece of fake data is used, not when a file is opened.
A decoy server is a whole system; this is a single file on a share.
A honeynet is a network of decoy systems.

stem: The IT manager of a law firm sees an alert: a paralegal opened "partner-bonuses.docx", a decoy that no task at the firm requires.
ask: Which of the following does this alert show?
options: The firm's real bonus data was stolen
An attacker used a fake password elsewhere
A decoy server was attacked from the internet
Someone browsed for data they did not need
why: The file is a decoy with fake contents; no real data was in it.
Use of fake data elsewhere is a honeytoken alert; here a file was opened.
An attack on a decoy server is a honeypot alert; here a file was opened.
No task needs the decoy, so opening it shows someone looking where they should not.

stem: After a honeyfile is placed on the HR share, a manager at a staffing agency says the real HR files on that share are now protected from theft.
ask: Which of the following corrects the manager?
options: The decoy encrypts the real files on the share
The decoy detects browsing but protects nothing
The decoy blocks anyone who opens a real file
The decoy moves real files to a safe place
why: A decoy changes nothing about the real files.
A honeyfile raises an alert when touched; it does not guard the real files beside it.
A honeyfile blocks no one; it only alerts when it is itself accessed.
A decoy moves nothing; the real files stay where they are.

stem: The security lead of a biotech firm wants an alert the moment anyone opens a tempting spreadsheet on the research share, whether or not anything inside it is ever used later.
ask: Which of the following BEST meets this goal?
why: A honeytoken is planted data whose use or sighting raises the alert; the goal is an alert on opening the file itself.
A honeyfile alerts on access, so opening the spreadsheet is enough.
File integrity monitoring alerts when a real file is changed, not when a tempting file is opened.
A honeynet is a network of decoy systems, not a file on a share.

stem: A security engineer at a city council must make a decoy file raise an alert when it is opened. The file server it sits on runs no monitoring agent.
ask: Which of the following could provide the alert?
options: A pressure mat under the file server
A camera aimed at the server rack
Renaming the file once a week
Content in the file that calls back on access
why: A mat senses weight on the floor, not a file being opened.
A camera watches the rack, not files opened over the network.
Renaming changes the bait but raises no alert.
A remote image or link inside the file contacts a monitor when the file is opened.

stem: A security analyst at a mediation firm reads the record below. The file named in it is a decoy with fake contents.
ask: Which of the following recorded this access?

lines: fs01 security log 2026-05-09 01:17 object access OPEN /srv/legal/clients/settlements-all.xlsx

options: A callback from content inside the file
A sign-in with a planted fake password
A scan alert from a decoy server
why: The record is the file server's own security log of the open, so file auditing on the server watched the honeyfile.
A callback reaches the alert service from the machine that opened the file; this record is the server's own log.
That is a honeytoken being used; the record shows a file opened, not a sign-in.
That is a honeypot alert; the record is an open of a file on the real file server.

stem: The deception lead at a regional newspaper wants honeyfiles to catch an intruder who is hunting through the network for something valuable.
ask: Where should the honeyfiles be placed?
options: On an isolated server no one can reach
On the public website for download
On file shares and admin desktops
Only on the security team's own laptops
why: A file no one can reach will never be opened by the intruder either.
Public downloads would bring alerts from anyone online, not only the intruder.
An intruder hunting for valuables browses shares and admin machines, so the bait belongs there.
Placing them only there leaves the shares and admin machines the intruder searches without any bait.

stem: A security trainer at a telecom company prepares a slide comparing honeyfiles with honeytokens.
ask: Which of the following statements belong on the slide? (Select TWO)
options: A honeyfile alerts only when its data is sold
A honeytoken is always a whole document
A honeyfile protects the real files near it
A honeyfile alerts when it is opened
A honeytoken alerts when its data is used
why: A honeyfile alerts on access; sightings of data elsewhere are a honeytoken trait.
A honeytoken is a piece of data such as a key or record, not a whole file.
A honeyfile detects browsing; it protects nothing.
Access to the file is the trigger.
Use or sighting of the fake data is the trigger.

ask: Which of the following describes the job of the Policy Administrator?
options: Carrying out the Policy Engine's decision
Making the grant or deny decision
Scoring the risk of each sign-in
why: The Policy Administrator acts on the decision by setting up or shutting down the path.
Deciding is the Policy Engine's job.
Adjusting checks to sign-in risk is adaptive identity.
The rules belong to policy-driven access control; the Policy Administrator acts on decisions.

ask: Which of the following can the Policy Administrator issue for an approved request?
why: The Policy Administrator can issue session tokens or credentials for the approved session.
Policies are defined by administrators and evaluated by the Policy Engine, not issued per session.
Device certificates come from the organization's certificate authority.
Risk scoring is part of deciding, not of setting up the session.

stem: Once the Policy Engine at a bank approves a teller's request, one component hands the gateway a session token and signals it to open the path.
ask: Which of the following components is described?
why: The Policy Engine already decided; the stem describes what happens next.
Adaptive identity is a way of judging risk, not a component that issues tokens.
Issuing the token and signaling the gateway to open the path is the Policy Administrator's job.
Threat scope reduction is a design goal, not a component that issues tokens.

stem: Midway through a session at a shipping firm, the Policy Engine withdraws its approval of a dispatcher's access.
ask: Which of the following components then signals the gateway to shut the session down?
why: The Policy Engine made the decision; it does not signal the gateway itself.
The Policy Administrator acts on the new decision by telling the gateway to close the path.
That is the rule framework, not a component that signals the gateway.
Adaptive identity adjusts verification; it does not shut sessions.

stem: A network engineer at a hospital asks which component creates the session credentials once a request to reach the imaging server has been approved.
ask: Which of the following components creates them?
why: The enforcement point receives instructions rather than issuing credentials.
The Policy Engine decides; acting on the decision is the Policy Administrator's job.
The requester and its device do not issue their own session credentials.
Creating session credentials and configuring the gateway is the Policy Administrator's role.

stem: At a water utility, one approved request must open a path through both an agent on the engineer's laptop and a gateway in front of the telemetry server.
ask: Which of the following components configures both?
why: The Policy Engine decides; it does not configure the enforcement points.
The agent and the gateway are themselves enforcement points being configured.
One decision can drive several enforcement points, and the Policy Administrator configures them.
The engineer and laptop are the requester, not the configuring component.

stem: A security architect at a university reads the term Policy Decision Point in NIST's Zero Trust guidance.
ask: Which of the following does that term cover?
options: Policy Engine plus Policy Enforcement Point
why: NIST groups the Policy Engine and Policy Administrator together as the Policy Decision Point.
The enforcement point is in the data plane and is not part of the decision point.
The enforcement point enforces; it is not part of the decision point.
The Policy Engine is also part of the decision point.

stem: A security architect at an insurer notes that the firm's Zero Trust product runs the decision logic and the session setup as one service on one server.
ask: Which of the following is accurate about this setup?
options: The Policy Administrator is no longer needed
The service now acts as the enforcement point
The Policy Engine now enforces traffic
Deciding and acting are still two roles
why: Its role, acting on decisions, still exists inside the service.
Enforcement still happens in the traffic path, at the enforcement point.
Combining services does not move enforcement to the decision maker.
Running the Policy Engine and Policy Administrator together does not merge their roles.

stem: A security analyst at an accounting firm finds the instructions below sent to the gateway in front of the ledger server.
ask: Which of the following components sent these instructions?

lines: 10:14:02 open session id=a71f subject=kosei resource=ledger.corp.example:443 ttl=3600

why: The Policy Engine decides; it does not send open and close instructions to the gateway.
Opening and closing sessions on the gateway is how the Policy Administrator acts on decisions.
The gateway is the enforcement point that receives these instructions.
kosei is the subject named in the instruction, not its sender.

ask: Which of the following does the Policy Administrator do? (Select TWO)
options: Makes the grant or deny decision
Sits in the traffic path to block traffic
Tells the PEP to open or close paths
why: Deciding is the Policy Engine's job.
That is the enforcement point.
It creates what the client needs for the approved session.
It configures the enforcement point over the control plane.
Administrators write the rules; the Policy Administrator acts on decisions.

ask: Which of the following describes the Policy Enforcement Point?
options: The component that makes grant or deny decisions
The component that issues tokens for sessions
The rule set that defines who may have access
The gatekeeper between subject and resource
why: Deciding is the Policy Engine's job.
Issuing tokens is the Policy Administrator's job.
The rule set is policy-driven access control.
The PEP sits between subject and resource and opens, monitors and closes connections.

ask: Which of the following parts of a Zero Trust architecture contains the Policy Enforcement Point?
why: The PEP takes instructions from the control plane but is not part of it.
The PEP sits in the traffic path, on the data plane.
The trust zone lies behind the PEP.
The Policy Engine is a separate decision component.

source.chapter: Zero Trust control plane vs data plane

stem: A control systems engineer at a paper mill notes that an appliance in front of the plant history server holds each new connection until it is told whether to allow or drop it.
ask: Which of the following Zero Trust components is the appliance?
why: The Policy Administrator gives the instruction; the appliance receives it.
The Policy Engine decides; the appliance waits to be told.
Holding connections and allowing or dropping them as instructed is enforcement.
That is the rule framework behind decisions, not a device that holds connections.

stem: Partway through a lesson at an online school, a gateway cuts a teacher's connection right after receiving an instruction to do so.
ask: Which of the following describes the gateway's part in this?
options: It carried out a decision it was given
It made the decision to end the session
It wrote the rule that ended the session
It requested access on the teacher's behalf
why: The PEP terminates connections as instructed; it does not decide.
Deciding is the Policy Engine's job; the gateway was told.
Rules are defined centrally, not by the gateway.
The teacher and device are the requester; the gateway stands between them and the resource.

stem: A network architect at a consulting firm drafts a Zero Trust design in which an agent on each laptop plus a gateway in front of the document server together play one role.
ask: Which of the following roles do the agent and the gateway share?
why: A PEP can be split into a client part on the device and a resource part in front of the server.
Neither part decides access.
Neither part issues tokens or instructs others.
The laptop is the system, but the agent on it enforces decisions.

stem: A security architect at a sports league must place the component that allows or blocks traffic to the ticketing app according to instructions it receives.
ask: Where should the architect place it?
options: Only on the separate control plane network
In the path between users and the app
On a backup server off site
why: Out of the traffic path, it could not block anything.
Inside the resource, traffic would already have arrived.
Every connection must pass the enforcement point for its decisions to apply.
A backup site sees none of the live traffic.

stem: A SOC analyst at a puzzle publisher needs live traffic counts for every approved session to the artwork server.
ask: Which of the following components is placed to report these counts?
why: The Policy Engine decides on the control plane and never sits in the traffic path.
The PEP sits in the path of every session and enables, monitors and ends connections.
The Policy Administrator sends instructions over the control plane; session traffic does not pass through it.
Each requester sees only its own session, not every session to the server.

stem: A training lead at a transit agency writes three verbs on a card for new staff: decide, act, enforce.
ask: Which of the following matches the components to these verbs in order?
why: This has the Administrator deciding; the Engine decides.
This has the PEP deciding, the classic mistake.
The Administrator acts on the decision and the PEP enforces, not the other way round.
The Policy Engine decides, the Policy Administrator acts and the PEP enforces.

source.chapter: Policy Engine vs Policy Administrator vs Policy Enforcement Point (Zero Trust components compared)

stem: A security analyst at a regional insurer reviews the gateway log below.
ask: Which of the following Zero Trust components wrote this log?
why: The reason names the Policy Administrator as the source of the instruction, not the writer of the log.
That is the rule framework behind the decision; it does not write gateway logs.
A gateway that monitors a session and terminates it when told is the enforcement point.
rmoss is the subject whose session was ended.

ask: Which of the following does a Policy Enforcement Point do? (Select TWO)
options: Makes the grant or deny decision
Passes requests on to the control plane
Opens and ends sessions as instructed
why: That is the Policy Engine.
The PEP forwards each request and waits for instructions.
The PEP enables, monitors and terminates connections when told.
That is the Policy Administrator.
Rules are defined centrally as part of policy-driven access control.

ask: Which of the following describes a honeynet?
options: Several linked decoys that imitate a real network
One decoy server built to look valuable
A fake document placed on a file share
A fake access key planted in source code
why: A honeynet is a network of honeypots and other decoys that together look like a real environment.
A single decoy server is a honeypot.
A decoy document is a honeyfile.
A planted fake key is a honeytoken.

ask: What can a honeynet show that a single honeypot cannot?
options: A first scan against one exposed system
Where stolen records end up later on
An attacker moving from system to system
Who opened a decoy document on a share
why: A single honeypot already shows a first scan.
Tracing stolen data is what honeytokens do.
With several connected decoys, defenders watch the attacker move laterally between them.
Opening a decoy document is what a honeyfile reports.

stem: Researchers at a university security lab want to watch how intruders move from a mail server to a payroll server and then to a backup server. No real systems may be put at risk.
ask: Which of the following should the researchers build?
why: One decoy system cannot show movement from one server to another.
A decoy file shows that someone opened it, not movement between servers.
A decoy credential shows that it was used, not the path across servers.
Several connected decoy servers let them watch the intruder move between systems.

stem: A deception engineer at an energy trader sees skilled attackers quickly leave a lone decoy server. She adds decoy workstations, a fake router and realistic traffic around it.
ask: Which of the following is the main gain from this change?
options: Real data for attackers to take
A lower cost than one decoy
why: Every added system is a decoy; nothing real is added.
There are now more decoy systems, all of which must stay isolated.
A whole decoy network looks more like a real environment than one server alone.
Several decoys cost more than one, not less.

stem: A department head at a software reseller asks whether the company's new honeynet includes any of its real servers.
ask: Which of the following answers the question?
options: Yes, it includes the real web servers
No, every system in it is a decoy
Yes, one real server anchors the rest
No, it is just one fake document
why: Real servers are never part of a honeynet.
A honeynet is built only from decoy resources.
Even one real server would put real data at risk; none is included.
A honeynet is a network of decoy systems, not a single document.

stem: A new network administrator at a magazine publisher confuses the company's honeynet with its screened subnet, where the public website runs.
ask: Which of the following describes the difference?
options: Only the honeynet consists entirely of decoys
Only the honeynet can face the internet
Only the screened subnet records attackers
Only the screened subnet must be isolated
why: A screened subnet holds real public services; a honeynet holds only decoys.
A screened subnet faces the internet too; that is where the public website runs.
Recording attacker activity is the main job of the honeynet.
A honeynet must be isolated from production as well.

stem: Over a month, the honeynet run by the threat hunting lead of a grocery chain records intruders moving from a decoy web server to a decoy file server with one stolen service account. She wants the production network to catch the same steps if they are ever tried there.
ask: Which of the following BEST uses the honeynet's findings?
options: Build detection rules from what it saw
Add more decoy servers to the honeynet
why: Blocking those addresses stops these sources, but the same steps from another address would go unseen.
Rules built from the captured path let the real network recognize the same steps from any source.
More decoys capture more, but they change nothing in the production network.
Linking them breaks the isolation and lets intruders reach real systems.

stem: A security engineer at a furniture retailer shares the deception design below with the IT manager.
ask: Which of the following does this design describe?

lines: segment:  isolated, no route to production
capture:  full packets and commands on every decoy

why: A honeypot is one decoy; this design links three.
Three connected decoy systems on an isolated segment form a honeynet.
A honeyfile is one decoy file, not connected systems.
A screened subnet holds real public services; this segment holds only decoys.

stem: The architect of a honeynet at a car rental company places it on a segment with no route to the production network.
ask: Which of the following explains this placement?
options: Attackers then cannot discover the honeynet at all
Malware brought in cannot reach real systems
The honeynet then needs no logging
why: The honeynet must still be found by attackers to be useful.
Isolation is about safety, not speed.
Isolation keeps anything an attacker drops on the decoys away from production.
Every decoy is still fully logged; that is the point of a honeynet.

stem: For a budget review, the security manager of a mining company compares a planned honeynet with the single honeypot the team runs today.
ask: Which of the following statements about the honeynet are accurate? (Select TWO)
options: It runs real services for customers
It needs no isolation from production
It costs more to build and keep believable
It can run as virtual machines on one host
It shows only an attacker's first contact
why: A honeynet holds only decoys.
A honeynet must be isolated so attackers cannot spread from it.
More decoys mean more work to keep them convincing.
A honeynet can be virtual, with the whole fake network on one physical host.
First contact is what a single honeypot shows; a honeynet also shows movement.

ask: Which of the following describes threat scope reduction?
options: Fewer entry points and least privilege
why: Learning about attackers is threat intelligence; it does not limit what they could reach.
Threat scope reduction shrinks the attack surface and gives subjects only the access they need.
Searching for attackers already inside is threat hunting.
Raising verification with risk is adaptive identity.

ask: What does threat scope reduction limit after an account is compromised?
options: How the attacker first made contact
How much the attacker can reach
How many logs the system keeps
why: The first contact has already happened; threat scope reduction limits what follows.
Password lifetime is not what threat scope reduction controls.
With fewer entry points and least privilege, a stolen account reaches little.
Log retention is an accounting matter.

stem: Warehouse supervisors at a furniture retailer used to get full network access over the VPN. Now they can reach only the inventory app, through a gateway.
ask: Which of the following Zero Trust concepts does this change apply?
why: Replacing full network access with one needed app shrinks what each account can reach.
Adaptive identity changes how much verification is asked, not what can be reached.
A gap analysis compares a program with a standard; it does not limit access.
No new factor was added; the change limits what the supervisors can reach.

stem: When the login of an order clerk at a beverage distributor was phished, the intruder found the account could open only the regional order app and nothing else.
ask: Which of the following limited the damage?
why: The account had only the access it needed, so the intruder's reach was small.
Nothing in the stem shows extra verification; the limit was on what the account could open.
The intruder got into the account; what limited the damage was how little it could open.
A gap analysis is a planning study; it does not limit an account.

stem: A security manager at an oil refinery says the new project will cut what any stolen account could touch. It will not look for attackers already inside, and it will not track attacker groups.
ask: Which of the following describes the project?
why: Looking for attackers already inside is threat hunting, which the stem rules out.
Tracking attacker groups is threat intelligence, which the stem rules out.
Cutting what a stolen account could touch is threat scope reduction.
MFA makes logins harder to steal; the project limits what a stolen login can touch.

stem: A network architect at a university hospital puts each clinical system behind its own enforcement point and removes administrator accounts that nobody uses.
ask: Which of the following goals do both changes serve?
why: Neither change alters how much verification a sign-in requires.
Separate enforcement points and fewer unused accounts both shrink what an attacker could reach.
Neither change proves who performed an action.
Neither change adds a sign-in factor.

stem: An infrastructure lead at a fintech company replaces permanent administrator rights with time-limited elevation granted for each task.
ask: Which of the following Zero Trust concepts does this support?
why: The change is about how long rights last, not how much verification is asked.
An enforcement point applies decisions in the traffic path; the change is about how long rights last.
Trust zones are areas behind enforcement points; the change is about admin rights.
Temporary rights mean a stolen admin account usually holds no standing access to abuse.

stem: A systems engineer at a seed company disables every service, port and account that the company's servers do not use.
ask: Which of the following is this an example of?
why: Nothing about sign-in verification changes.
Nothing here proves who did what.
Removing unused services, ports and accounts cuts the entry points an attacker could use.
No sign-in factor is added.

stem: A network administrator at a hotel chain changes the remote access rule below for outside contractors.
ask: Which of the following does the change achieve?

lines: rule 14 (new): permit group=vendors dst=203.0.113.25 port=443 hours=8

options: Less reach for a stolen vendor login
Stronger proof of each vendor's identity
A record of each vendor's session
why: The group now reaches one host on one port for a limited time instead of a whole network.
The rule does not change how vendors authenticate.
Recording sessions is accounting; the rule limits destinations.
The rule names destinations and ports; it does not encrypt anything.

ask: Which of the following support threat scope reduction? (Select TWO)
why: Giving only the access a task needs limits what a compromise can reach.
Feeds tell defenders about attackers; they do not limit reach.
Password lifetime does not limit what an account can reach.
Separating resources keeps an attacker in one place from reaching the rest.
A flat network is a large trust zone, the opposite of reducing scope.

ask: Which of the following describes an ultrasonic sensor?
options: A sensor that sends inaudible sound and reads echoes
A sensor that emits microwaves and reads the reflections
A sensor that takes in body heat and emits nothing
A sensor that closes a circuit when stepped on
why: An ultrasonic sensor sends out sound beyond human hearing and detects movement from changes in the echoes.
Reflected microwaves are how a microwave sensor works.
Taking in heat is how an infrared sensor works.
Reacting to being stepped on is how a pressure sensor works.

ask: Which of the following does an ultrasonic sensor use to detect motion?
why: Ultrasonic sensors work with sound, not light or heat.
Radio waves are used by microwave sensors.
Body heat is sensed by infrared sensors.
Ultrasonic sensors do not use light.

stem: An alarm technician explains that the unit in the repair room of a music store sends out a tone above human hearing. It raises an alarm when the returning echoes change.
ask: Which sensor is installed in the repair room?
why: A microwave sensor sends radio pulses, not a tone.
A tone above human hearing and a change in its echoes describe an ultrasonic sensor.
A passive infrared sensor sends out nothing; it senses heat.
A pressure sensor reacts to weight and sends out nothing.

stem: At a tailoring shop, the ultrasonic sensor in the fabric store raised an alarm overnight. The owner asks what the sensor actually detected.
ask: Which of the following did the sensor detect?
options: A change in the echoes of its sound
A change in the reflected radio waves
why: Body heat is what an infrared sensor detects.
Weight is what a pressure sensor detects.
An ultrasonic sensor detects movement from changes in the echo pattern of its sound.
Reflected radio waves are what a microwave sensor reads.

stem: A receptionist at a dental clinic worries that the new ultrasonic motion sensor in the waiting room will bother patients with noise.
ask: Which of the following answers her concern?
options: It makes its noise only during the night
It uses light instead of sound
It uses heat instead of sound
Its sound is too high for people to hear
why: It emits the same sound day and night, and people never hear it.
An ultrasonic sensor uses sound, not light.
Using heat would make it an infrared sensor; ultrasonic uses sound.
Ultrasonic sensors emit sound beyond human hearing.

stem: The records officer of a ship registry learns that the passive infrared detector in the deed room missed an installer on a walk test, because he crossed a gap between its zones. She wants a different kind of sensor that fills the whole enclosed room evenly and does not react to forklifts in the warehouse beyond the room's plywood wall.
ask: Which of the following should the records officer choose?
why: Microwave covers large areas, but its energy passes through plywood, so the forklifts next door could set it off.
Its sound fills the enclosed room, reaching spots heat zones miss, and it does not pass through the wall.
A pressure mat covers one spot, not the whole room.
Infrared watches separate zones and can miss a gap between them, which is the problem the walk test found.

stem: The studio manager of a pottery school sees that the ultrasonic detector in the glaze store raises false alarms only on windy nights, when no one is inside. The unit hangs beside the outside door, which has a wide gap under it.
ask: Which of the following would fix these false alarms?
options: Point the unit straight at the door
Seal the gap under the door
Add a pressure mat by the door
why: Aiming it at the door puts the draft right in its path, which makes the problem worse.
Higher sensitivity makes the unit react to even smaller disturbances.
Strong drafts disturb ultrasonic motion detectors, so openings near the unit should be sealed.
A mat adds another sensor but leaves the ultrasonic unit's false alarms as they are.

stem: A procurement officer at a hospital supply company checks a draft product sheet for an ultrasonic motion detector before it is printed. A writer pasted one claim from the sheet of a different kind of sensor.
ask: Which claim on the sheet is wrong for this detector?

lines: Detects: frequency shift of the returned echo
Coverage: one enclosed room up to 7 m
Ignores: movement beyond the room's walls

options: That it reads changes in the echo
That it covers one closed room
That it ignores movement outside the room
That it sends out nothing at all
why: An ultrasonic unit does read changes in the echo of its own sound, so this claim is right.
An ultrasonic unit fills an enclosed room with its sound, so this claim is right.
Its sound does not pass through walls, so movement outside the room is not sensed; this claim is right.
An ultrasonic unit is active: it sends out sound above human hearing and listens for the echoes, so it cannot send out nothing.

stem: At a translation agency, two side-by-side offices each have a glass wall facing the same corridor. One office has an ultrasonic motion unit and the other a microwave unit. When the night guard walks the corridor, only one office raises an alarm.
ask: Which of the following explains the alarm?
options: The ultrasonic unit's sound passes the glass
The microwave unit's radio waves pass the glass
The microwave unit senses the guard's body heat
The ultrasonic unit senses the guard's weight
why: Ultrasonic sound does not pass glass, so the ultrasonic unit stays inside its office.
Microwave units use radio waves, which pass through glass, so that unit also sees the corridor.
Sensing body heat is how an infrared sensor works; a microwave unit reads radio echoes.
Sensing weight is how a pressure sensor works; an ultrasonic unit reads sound echoes.

stem: The owner of a hardware store reads the manual for the new ultrasonic sensor in the key-cutting room.
ask: Which of the following statements about the sensor are accurate? (Select TWO)
options: It works only while the lights are on
It sends out sound above human hearing
Its sound does not pass through the walls
It detects people by their body heat
It reads changes in radio reflections
why: Sound needs no light, so it works in the dark.
Ultrasonic means sound beyond what people can hear.
The sound stays inside the room.
Body heat is what infrared senses.
Radio reflections are what microwave sensors read.

ask: Which of the following describes bollards?
options: A two-door booth that admits one person at a time
A tall barrier that keeps people off a whole site
Short, sturdy posts that stop cars but let walkers pass
A floor mat that reports weight placed on it
why: That is an access control vestibule, which controls people at a door, not vehicles.
That describes a fence along a perimeter; bollards let people walk between them.
Bollards are short, strong posts spaced so a vehicle cannot pass but a person on foot can.
That is a pressure sensor, which detects a person rather than stopping a vehicle.

ask: What is a row of bollards designed to stop?
why: Bollards leave gaps so people on foot can pass; they are not meant to stop them.
Bollards are spaced and anchored to stop cars and trucks.
Someone following another person through a door is stopped by an access control vestibule.
People climbing over a boundary are slowed by a tall fence, not by short posts.

stem: The manager of a garden center wants to keep cars in the parking lot from being driven into the glass front of the greenhouse. Shoppers must still be able to walk in freely.
ask: Which of the following should the manager install?
options: A row of short steel posts
A badge reader on the door
why: Short steel posts block a car but leave gaps that shoppers walk through.
An entry booth controls one person at a time at a door; it does nothing about cars.
A tall barrier would also keep shoppers out, which the manager does not want.
A badge reader controls who opens a door; it cannot stop a car hitting the glass.

stem: A planner at a transit authority places short steel posts outside a busy station so that no car can drive into the crowd. The posts are spaced so that riders move in an orderly line toward the ticket gates.
ask: Which other purpose do the posts serve in this design?
options: Guiding the movement of people on foot
Holding each rider for an identity check
Recording which riders enter the station
Detecting riders who carry metal objects
why: Bollards can also channel foot traffic, here into a line toward the gates.
Holding a person for a check is what a two-door vestibule does, not a row of posts.
Posts record nothing; a camera or badge system would keep a record.
Posts sense nothing; they are passive physical barriers.

stem: After steel posts are installed in front of a pharmacy, an auditor notes that they do nothing to stop a person who walks up to the door. The store manager asks whether the posts were a mistake.
ask: Which of the following explains why the posts still serve their purpose?
options: They are meant to record who walks past
They are meant to stop vehicles, not people
They are meant to hold each visitor for a check
They are meant to alert staff when touched
why: Posts record nothing, so this cannot be their purpose.
Bollards are built to stop cars; letting people walk past them is by design.
Posts hold no one; a two-door vestibule does that at a door.
Plain posts raise no alert; they are a passive barrier.

stem: The facilities manager of a city library must keep vehicles off the paved plaza in front of the building. A delivery van still has to reach the loading door across the plaza each morning.
ask: Which of the following meets both needs?
options: Fixed bollards across the whole plaza
A fence around the whole plaza
Fixed bollards with one that can be lowered
A camera watching the whole plaza
why: Fixed posts everywhere would also block the delivery van every morning.
A fence would keep library visitors off the plaza as well.
Fixed posts keep vehicles out, and the one that lowers lets the van through when staff allow it.
A camera records vehicles on the plaza but does not stop them.

stem: A facilities engineer at a data center must protect the outdoor generators and fuel tank that sit beside the service road. The concern is a delivery truck that misjudges a turn and strikes them.
ask: Which of the following controls should the engineer install?
why: A fence controls people along a perimeter; it is not built to stop a truck.
Cameras would record the crash but not prevent it.
A pressure sensor reports weight at a spot; it cannot stop a truck.
Anchored posts stop a vehicle before it reaches the equipment.

stem: A project manager at a convention center receives the contractor's work order below.
ask: Which threat does this work order address?

lines: Item 1  Set 18 steel posts along the main walkway to the doors
Item 2  Anchor each post in concrete, rated for impact
Item 3  Keep 1.5 m between posts for strollers and wheelchairs

why: Following someone through a door is stopped by a vestibule, not by posts outside.
Climbing a boundary is slowed by a tall fence; posts with gaps let people through.
Impact-rated posts with walking gaps are bollards, which stop vehicles.
Darkness is fixed with lighting; steel posts do not light anything.

stem: The court security officer of a county courthouse must stop a vehicle driven at speed from reaching the crowded waiting area behind the front windows. Two suppliers offer steel posts that look alike, but only one supplier's posts have been tested against a vehicle of a stated weight and speed.
ask: Which of the following describes the risk of choosing the untested posts?
options: They may not hold against a heavy truck
They will block people walking to the door
They cannot be lowered to let deliveries in
They leave gaps wide enough for a car
why: Posts are rated by testing them against a set vehicle weight and speed; an unrated post may stop little.
Spacing, not testing, decides whether people on foot can pass between posts.
Whether a post can be lowered depends on its design, fixed or retractable, not on whether it was tested.
Spacing is set when the posts are installed; testing tells whether a post holds, not how far apart posts stand.

stem: A parks department planner proposes a row of steel bollards between a playground and the busy road beside it.
ask: Which of the following statements about the planned bollards are accurate? (Select TWO)
options: They hold each person for an identity check
They alert staff when someone climbs over
They keep cars from reaching the playground
They let children and parents walk between them
They record who enters the playground
why: That is a vestibule at a door, not posts along a road.
Bollards raise no alert, and they are not meant to be climbed over.
Stopping vehicles is what bollards are built for.
Bollards are spaced so people on foot can pass.
Posts keep no record; a camera would.

ask: Which of the following describes policy-driven access control?
options: Access granted to anything on the inside network
More verification asked when sign-in risk rises
Fewer entry points and less standing access
Access decided by rules on identity and context
why: Granting by network location is what policy-driven access control replaces.
Adjusting verification to risk is adaptive identity.
Shrinking entry points and access is threat scope reduction.
Defined policies that combine identity, context and rules decide each request.

ask: Which of the following components evaluates the policies in policy-driven access control?
why: The Policy Administrator carries out the decision; it does not evaluate the policies.
The Policy Engine evaluates the policies for each request and makes the decision.
Adaptive identity is a concept for adjusting verification, not the component that evaluates policy.
Threat scope reduction is a design goal, not a component that evaluates policy.

stem: A rule set by the security team at a regional bank lets loan officers reach the loan system only from managed devices on weekdays.
ask: Which of the following Zero Trust concepts is this rule an example of?
why: The Policy Administrator carries out decisions; it is not the rule itself.
A defined rule combining role, device and time decides access.
Nothing in the rule changes how much verification is asked.
The rule names no sign-in factors; it sets conditions for access.

stem: A network engineer at a university is retiring the old rule that anyone on the campus network may reach the grades server. Each request will now be judged by rules on identity and device.
ask: Which of the following describes the change?
options: Access now depends only on location
Access is now logged for billing
Access now waits for a gap analysis
Access now depends on policy, not location
why: Location-based access is the old rule being retired.
Logging is accounting; the change is about how access is decided.
A gap analysis is a planning study, not a per-request decision.
The new rules use identity and device instead of being on campus.

stem: A compliance officer at a pharmaceutical firm asks whether the employee handbook's security policy is the "policy" meant by policy-driven access control.
ask: Which of the following answers the officer accurately?
options: No; it means rules a system evaluates
Yes; the handbook is checked on each request
Yes; any written document is such a policy
No; it means the firewall's hardware
why: Here policy means rules a system evaluates per request; a handbook is a managerial document.
A handbook is not evaluated by the system for each request.
Written policy documents are managerial controls, not machine-evaluated rules.
Policy here is a rule set, not a piece of hardware.

stem: A security architect at a retail chain moves the access rules kept separately in 40 applications into one central rule set.
ask: Which of the following is a direct benefit of this change?
options: Users no longer need to authenticate
Traffic no longer passes through a gateway
The same request gets the same answer everywhere
why: Central rules still need a proven identity to evaluate.
Enforcement still happens in the traffic path.
One central rule set gives consistent decisions across the environment.
Rules can still require healthy devices; centralizing them removes nothing.

stem: A threat feed warns the security manager of a regional airline that a partner firm's staff accounts were breached. Within minutes, every partner account must be shut out of all 30 internal apps.
ask: Which of the following benefits of policy-driven access control makes this possible?
options: Each sign-in prompt adapts to risk
Auditors can read why each grant was made
One rule change takes effect in every app at once
why: Adapting prompts to risk is adaptive identity; it asks for more verification and does not shut a group of accounts out of every app.
The partner accounts are not admitted by location, so ending location trust would not shut them out.
Reading the reasons for past grants shuts no one out now.
With the rules held centrally, one change to them applies across all 30 apps at once.

stem: A security analyst at a software startup finds that one internal app grants access to anyone on the office Wi-Fi, while every other app checks role and device health.
ask: Which of the following should replace the Wi-Fi based grant?
options: A central rule on identity and posture
A longer session time for that app
why: Access would still depend on being on the network.
A defined rule on identity and context brings the app in line with policy-driven access control.
Access would still depend on network location.
Session length does not change how access is decided.

stem: A security engineer at a regional newspaper reviews the central rule below for the payroll system.
ask: Which of the following requests does this rule allow?
options: A payroll clerk on a personal phone at 10:00
An editor on a managed laptop at 10:00
A payroll clerk on a managed laptop at 10:00
A payroll clerk on a managed laptop at 21:00
why: A personal phone fails the managed device condition.
An editor fails the Payroll role condition.
The role, the managed device and the hour all meet the rule.
21:00 is outside the allowed hours.

ask: Which of the following statements about policy-driven access control are accurate? (Select TWO)
options: Each app keeps its own unwritten rules
It removes the need for authentication
The Policy Engine evaluates the rules
why: That is the location-based trust it replaces.
Policies use who is asking plus conditions such as device and time.
Rules are defined and managed centrally.
Identity must still be proven for the rules to use it.
The Policy Engine applies the policies to each request.

ask: Which of the following describes the purpose of physical security?
options: Limiting what a signed-in user is allowed to do
Proving who a user is before granting sign-in
Protecting sites, equipment and people from intrusion
Showing that stored data has not been altered
why: That is authorization, enforced in software after sign-in, not by barriers, guards or sensors.
That is authentication of a user, a check made by a system, not a physical control.
Physical security keeps buildings, equipment and people safe from physical access and harm.
That is integrity, kept by checks on the data itself, not by protecting a building.

ask: Which of the following explains why physical controls are placed in several rings around a protected asset?
options: An intruder must defeat one control after another
One strong control can then replace all the others
No ring then needs to be watched or tested
Each control can then serve only a single goal
why: With layers, getting past one control still leaves the next one in the way.
Rings work because no single control is trusted alone, so nothing is replaced.
Rings still need watching and testing; layering adds controls, it does not remove upkeep.
Layering says nothing about one goal per control; many physical controls serve several goals.

stem: The operations manager of a textile mill plans three rings of protection: the outer boundary, the entrance to the mill building, and the dye lab inside. For the middle ring she needs a control that checks each person who comes into the building.
ask: Which of the following belongs in the middle ring?
options: A fence along the outer boundary
A guard checking IDs at the door
Locks on the dye lab cabinets
why: A fence belongs to the outer ring; it marks the boundary but checks no one coming into the building.
Lighting belongs to the outer ring; it helps people see the grounds but checks no one at the entrance.
A guard at the building entrance checks each person before they come in, which is the job of the middle ring.
Cabinet locks guard the equipment in the innermost ring, not the way into the building.

source.chapter: Physical access controls compared (bollards vs fencing vs access control vestibule vs guards vs badges)

stem: The security manager of a coin mint plans protection for its vault: a perimeter fence, then a guarded front entrance, then an access control vestibule at the vault door.
ask: Which of the following describes the approach in this plan?
options: One control chosen to cover every threat
Several rings of controls around one asset
Controls added only after an incident occurs
Every control placed at the same doorway
why: The plan uses three controls in sequence, not a single control.
Fence, entrance and vault door form rings, so an intruder meets one control after another.
The stem describes a plan made in advance, not controls added after harm.
The controls sit at the perimeter, the entrance and the vault, three different places.

source.chapter: Physical access controls compared (bollards vs fencing vs access control vestibule vs guards vs badges)

stem: An office manager at a small law firm worries that a visitor could carry the file server out of the building. She asks for a locked server room, a door alarm and a receptionist who signs visitors in.
ask: Which of the following concepts do the requested controls belong to?
why: Authorization models decide what a signed-in user may do in software; they cannot stop hardware leaving a room.
A locked room, a door alarm and a person at reception protect equipment from physical access.
Non-repudiation proves who performed an action; it does not keep a server inside the building.
Gap analysis compares current and target security; the requested items are controls, not a comparison.

stem: A new security analyst at an insurance office tells a colleague that the motion sensors and cameras in the office prevent break-ins.
ask: Which of the following corrects the analyst's statement?
options: They stop break-ins only during the night
They repair the damage after a break-in
They only discourage intruders who see them
They reveal break-ins rather than stop them
