stem: The facilities lead of a call center installs passive infrared sensors on the call floor to cover it at night.
ask: Which of the following statements about these sensors are accurate? (Select TWO)
options: They work with the lights switched off
They sense through the glass partitions
They record video of each event
They sense the heat of a moving body
why: Sensing heat needs no light, so they work in the dark.
Infrared does not pass through glass.
They record no images; cameras do that.
Sending radio pulses is how microwave sensors work; passive infrared sends nothing.
Infrared sensors detect body heat.

source.chapter: Infrared sensors (passive infrared, PIR motion detectors)

ask: Which of the following describes the subject in a Zero Trust architecture?
options: The resource that is being accessed
The gateway that enforces each decision
The service that makes each decision
The user, app or process requesting access
why: The resource is what the subject wants to reach, not the subject.
The gateway is the Policy Enforcement Point.
The decision maker is the Policy Engine.
The subject is whoever or whatever asks for access, human or not.

ask: Which of the following describes where the subject/system sits relative to the Policy Enforcement Point?
options: Inside the trust zone behind the PEP
In the control plane, beside the PEP
On the untrusted side, before the PEP
Behind the resource it is requesting
why: Only entities that have passed the enforcement point are in the trust zone.
The subject/system is part of the data plane.
The requester has not yet passed the enforcement point.
The requester reaches the resource through the enforcement point, not from behind it.

stem: A storage administrator at a museum notes that a backup service account requests write access to a storage interface every night. No person is involved in the request.
ask: Which of the following roles does the backup service play in this request?
why: A non-human entity such as a service that requests access is a subject.
The storage interface is the resource being requested.
The Policy Engine decides on the request; it does not make it.
The enforcement point stands between requester and resource.

stem: A field engineer at a power company uses a company tablet to open the maintenance app.
ask: Which of the following labels the engineer and the tablet correctly?
why: The engineer is the person requesting access, so the engineer is never the system.
The resource is the maintenance app, not the tablet.
The engineer is requesting access, not being accessed.
The person requesting is the subject, and the device used is the system.

stem: A sales engineer at a solar installer opens the quoting app from her managed company laptop and gets full access. Minutes later, from her personal phone, the same account gets read-only access.
ask: Which of the following explains the different results?
options: The account that made the request
The device the request came from
The gateway in front of the app
why: The same account made both requests, so the account cannot explain the difference.
The device is checked along with the account; the managed laptop got full access and the personal phone got less.
She asked for the same quoting app both times.
The gateway enforces the decision it is given; it does not decide, so it does not explain the difference.

stem: A security architect at an insurer warns that checking only the user ignores a compromised laptop, and checking only the laptop ignores a stolen account.
ask: Which of the following does the architect want evaluated on each request?
options: The account and the laptop together
Only the laptop the request comes from
why: That misses a compromised laptop, as the architect warns.
Evaluating both covers a stolen account and a compromised laptop.
That misses a stolen account, as the architect warns.
The app is what is protected; the requester and its device still need checking.

stem: A help desk lead at a tutoring company tells new hires that a subject in Zero Trust is always a human being.
ask: Which of the following corrects the lead?
options: Subjects sit in the control plane
Services and processes can be subjects too
why: People and services request access as subjects too, so subjects are not only devices.
The resource is what is being accessed, not the requester.
Subjects are part of the data plane.
Applications, services and other non-human entities can request access as subjects.

stem: A network architect at a casino draws the requester and its device on the company's Zero Trust diagram.
ask: Which of the following parts of the architecture holds them?
why: The subject/system is part of the data plane.
The control plane holds the decision makers.
The trust zone lies behind the enforcement point; the requester has not passed it yet.
The Policy Engine is a control plane component that judges the requester.

source.chapter: Zero Trust control plane vs data plane

stem: A security analyst at a lending company reviews the access request record below.
ask: Which of the following does this record show was evaluated along with the service account?
options: A multifactor sign-in by a person
A verdict from a threat intelligence feed
The state of the host it came from
The network location of the requester
why: The requester is a service account, and the record shows no sign-in factor.
The record names no threat feed or verdict.
The record shows srv-app-07 was checked as managed and patched, so the device was weighed along with the account.
The record names a host, but no network or location.

ask: Which of the following can act as a subject in Zero Trust? (Select TWO)
options: A service account calling an API
why: A human user requesting access is a subject.
That is the resource.
The Policy Engine decides on requests; it is not the requester.
A trust zone is an area, not a requester.
Non-human entities that request access are subjects too.

ask: Which of the following does non-repudiation provide?
options: Proof that data was unchanged, with no proof of sender
Proof of who sent data, which the sender cannot deny
Assurance that data stays secret in transit
Assurance that a service stays reachable
why: That is what a hash alone gives: integrity without proof of who made it.
Non-repudiation proves the origin and integrity of data so the sender cannot credibly deny it.
Keeping data secret is confidentiality, not proof of origin.
Keeping a service reachable is availability, not proof of origin.

ask: Which of the following explains why a shared symmetric key cannot provide non-repudiation?
options: Symmetric keys are too short to trust
Symmetric keys cannot detect any changes
Either key holder could have made the output
Symmetric keys only protect stored data
why: Key length is not the issue; the problem is that the key is shared.
Shared-key methods such as HMAC do reveal changes; their weakness is that two parties hold the key.
The key is shared, so the output could come from either party and points to no single sender.
Symmetric keys protect data in transit as well; the problem is that the key is shared.

stem: A sales director at a printing company insists he never sent a price quote that a customer received from his account. The company wants proof of the sender that an outside party can check.
ask: Which of the following would have given the company that proof?
options: A digital signature on the quote
A redundant copy of the quote
why: Only the director's private key could create the signature, and anyone with his public key can verify it.
Anyone can compute a hash, so it shows the quote is unchanged but not who sent it.
Encryption keeps the quote secret; it does not prove who sent it.
A second copy keeps the quote available; it proves nothing about the sender.

stem: A release engineer at a game studio publishes a hash beside each download so players can check for tampering. A partner asks whether the hashes also prove the studio produced the files.
ask: Which of the following is accurate about the published hashes?
options: They prove integrity but not origin
They prove both integrity and origin
They keep the files secret from players
They keep the download site reachable
why: Anyone can compute a hash, so it gives integrity but not proof of origin.
A hash proves integrity only; proving origin needs a private key, as in a digital signature.
A hash does not hide the files; secrecy is confidentiality.
A hash does nothing for availability.

stem: A loan officer at a bank approves wire transfers in a system that shares one secret key with every officer. If an approval is disputed later, an auditor must be able to confirm exactly which officer approved it.
ask: Which of the following should replace the shared key approach?
why: An HMAC uses a shared key, so the system or any key holder could have produced the tag.
A hash shows the approval is unchanged but says nothing about who approved it.
Each officer signs with a private key no one else holds, so the auditor can tie each approval to one officer.
A shared symmetric key cannot single out one officer, and encryption hides data rather than proving origin.

stem: A contracts manager at an engineering firm receives a supplier agreement signed with the supplier's private key. She checks the signature with the supplier's public key, and it verifies.
ask: Which of the following does the successful check show?
options: The agreement was kept secret in transit
Its origin is proven and its text is unaltered
Anyone holding the public key could have signed it
Only the contracts manager can read it
why: A signature does not encrypt; secrecy in transit is confidentiality.
Only the supplier's private key could make a signature that verifies with its public key, and any change would break it.
The public key only verifies; signing needs the private key, which only the supplier holds.
The signature does not restrict who can read the agreement.

stem: A security officer at a notary service learns that a notary's private signing key was copied from an unprotected laptop last month.
ask: Which of the following is the main effect on documents signed with that key since then?
options: Their contents are now readable by anyone
Their signatures will no longer verify
Their hashes no longer match the documents
The signer can credibly deny making them
why: A signature never hid the contents, so the copied key changes nothing about secrecy.
The signatures still verify with the public key; the problem is that someone else could have made them.
Copying a key does not change the documents, so their hashes still match.
Once someone else holds the key, a valid signature no longer proves the notary made it.

stem: A quality lead at a drug research lab has each scientist digitally sign the entries in an electronic lab notebook. Later, no scientist must be able to claim credibly that a colleague signed an entry in his or her name.
ask: Where should each scientist's private signing key be kept?
options: In a folder the whole lab can read
On a lab server, one key for the team
On the scientist's own smart card
With the scientist, plus a copy for the lab head
why: Any colleague could copy the key from the folder and sign, so a scientist could credibly blame someone else.
A key the whole team signs with cannot single out one scientist as the signer.
A key held in hardware by one scientist alone means only that scientist could have made the signature.
A second holder of the key could have signed too, so the scientist could deny the signature.

stem: A buyer at a hardware wholesaler opens an emailed price change and sees the status lines below.
ask: Which of the following does this email provide?

lines: Certificate issuer: Supplier Example Issuing CA

why: A valid signature tied to the sender's certificate proves who sent it, so the sender cannot credibly deny it.
The last line shows no encryption, so the email was not kept secret.
Nothing in the lines concerns keeping a service reachable.
Accounting logs what users did on a system; a signed email is not an access log.

ask: Which of the following statements about non-repudiation are accurate? (Select TWO)
options: An HMAC tag can provide it
It depends on the private key staying private
A plain hash can provide it
A digital signature can provide it
why: An HMAC uses a shared key, so either party could have made the tag.
If the private key is stolen, the signer can credibly deny the signature.
Anyone can compute a hash, so it proves integrity only.
Encryption gives confidentiality; non-repudiation comes from signing.
A signature made with a private key proves who signed and that nothing changed.

ask: Which of the following describes adaptive identity?
options: One fixed login check for every request
Sharing one login across many systems
Verification that changes with context and risk
Limiting each user to the apps needed
why: A fixed check is what adaptive identity replaces.
Sharing a login across systems is single sign-on, not adaptive identity.
Adaptive identity uses context such as location, device and behavior to decide how much verification to ask for.
Limiting reach is threat scope reduction.

ask: How should adaptive identity treat a usual office login compared with a login from an unknown device in another country?
options: Ask less of the office login
Ask the same of both logins
Ask more of the office login
why: The office login matches normal context, so it needs less verification than the risky one.
Treating both alike ignores the context that adaptive identity weighs.
The unknown device abroad is the riskier login, so it gets more checks.
Both logins still need authentication; only the amount changes.

stem: A clinical researcher at a university usually signs in from a lab desktop. At 3 a.m. her account signs in from an unfamiliar laptop on a hotel network, and the system demands an extra MFA prompt.
ask: Which of the following Zero Trust concepts is shown?
why: Threat scope reduction limits what an account can reach; here the amount of verification changed.
A gap analysis compares a program with a standard; it does not run at sign-in.
Non-repudiation proves who sent something; it does not change login checks.
An unusual time, device and network raised the risk, so the system asked for more verification.

stem: An IT manager at a law firm notes that partners on their usual office laptops are not prompted again, but the same accounts on new devices must complete an extra check.
ask: Which of the following is the benefit of this approach?
options: Every user gets the same prompts
Prompts only where risk is higher
why: The stem shows prompts differ by device, so they are not the same for all.
Friction is applied to the unusual sign-ins, not to every sign-in.
Adaptive identity changes how much is asked, not whether users authenticate.
Office laptops are not prompted again, but the users still authenticated.

stem: A security architect at an online brokerage wants each sign-in scored low, medium or high risk from device, location and behavior. Medium risk must prompt a fresh MFA, and high risk must be blocked.
ask: Which of the following Zero Trust concepts BEST describes this requirement?
why: Central rules decide access, but the stem stresses verification that changes with risk.
Verification that rises with the risk of each sign-in is adaptive identity.
It limits what an account can reach; the stem is about how much verification is asked.
The enforcement point applies decisions in the traffic path; it does not score sign-in risk.

stem: Partway through a session, a finance user at a manufacturer starts downloading thousands of records from a new location, and the system asks the user to authenticate again.
ask: Which of the following explains the new prompt?
options: The session token expired on schedule
Risk is re-checked during the session
why: The stem ties the prompt to the unusual download and location, not to a timer.
A deleted account would be refused, not asked to authenticate again.
Accounting records activity; it does not require new logins.
Adaptive identity keeps watching; unusual behavior mid-session can trigger re-authentication.

stem: A help desk analyst at a sporting goods retailer describes adaptive identity to a new colleague as the same thing as single sign-on.
ask: Which of the following corrects the analyst?
options: It adjusts checks to risk; SSO shares one login
It is SSO with a stronger password
It shares one login; SSO adjusts checks
It is a fourth factor that SSO lacks
why: Adaptive identity changes how much verification is asked; single sign-on reuses one login across systems.
Adaptive identity is not a form of single sign-on.
This swaps the two: single sign-on is the one that shares a login.
Adaptive identity decides when to ask for factors; it is not a factor itself.

stem: At a streaming service, a full-time video editor and a visiting contract editor sign in from the same managed workstation, in the same office, at the same hour. The contractor is asked for an extra MFA prompt, and the employee is not.
ask: Which of the following signals caused the different treatment?
options: The office each person was in
The tie each person has to the company
The hour each person signed in
why: Both used the same managed workstation, so the device cannot explain the difference.
Both signed in from the same office, so location cannot explain the difference.
Adaptive identity weighs the relationship to the organization; a visiting contractor gets more verification than a full-time employee.
Both signed in at the same hour, so time cannot explain the difference.

stem: A security engineer at a media company compares two sign-in records below for the same account.
ask: Which of the following explains why request 5518 was asked for MFA?
options: Its device failed a health check
Its user lacks the needed role
Its network raised the risk score
why: Both records show the same managed, compliant laptop, so the device did not change the score.
Both records show password=ok, so the password was accepted.
It is the same user on both records, and a missing role would end in a denial, not an MFA prompt.
The only change is the network: a hosting provider range instead of the office, which adaptive identity weighs as riskier and answers with a fresh MFA prompt.

ask: Which of the following describe adaptive identity? (Select TWO)
options: Steps up authentication when risk rises
Uses context such as device and location
Gives one fixed prompt to every request
Shares one login across many apps
why: Higher risk brings more verification.
Context and risk signals decide how much verification is needed.
A fixed prompt for everyone is what adaptive identity replaces.
That is single sign-on.
Recording sessions is accounting.

ask: Which of the following describes fencing as a physical control?
options: A barrier that marks and guards a perimeter
Posts that stop vehicles but let walkers pass
Two doors that open only one at a time
A card that unlocks doors and logs each use
why: Fencing marks a boundary and keeps people out of the area inside it.
That is bollards, which control vehicles at one frontage.
That is an access control vestibule at a single doorway.
That is an access badge, used at doors, not along a boundary.

ask: Which kind of fence lets guards and cameras watch the grounds on its other side?
why: A transparent fence such as mesh or chain link lets people and cameras see through it.
Solid boards are opaque, so they block the view.
A brick wall is opaque and hides what is behind it.
Solid panels are opaque and block the view.

stem: The estate manager of a vineyard wants to clearly mark where the private grounds begin. The barrier should also slow down hikers who wander in from the public trail.
ask: Which of the following controls fits this need?
why: Bollards stop vehicles and leave gaps for walkers, so hikers would pass straight through.
A fence marks the boundary and delays people on foot crossing it.
A vestibule controls one building door, not the edge of open grounds.
A badge opens doors for staff; it does not mark or guard a boundary.

stem: The security manager of an aircraft maker wants drivers on the public road to be unable to see the prototype work in the test yard.
ask: Which of the following should the manager choose for the yard?
why: Chain link is transparent, so drivers could still see the work.
Bollards stop vehicles but block no one's view.
An opaque fence hides activity inside from anyone outside.
A camera records the gate; it hides nothing from the road.

stem: A site supervisor for a water utility finds marks showing that someone climbed the low fence around a pumping station overnight.
ask: Which of the following changes would make the fence harder to cross?
options: Replacing it with a see-through mesh
Placing steel posts along its base
Putting a camera at the main gate
Raising it and adding razor wire on top
why: See-through mesh changes what can be seen, not how hard the fence is to climb.
Posts at the base stop vehicles, not a person climbing over.
A camera at the gate records; it does not stop someone climbing elsewhere.
Height and razor wire make a fence harder to climb.

stem: The yard manager of a lumber dealer learns that thieves cut through the perimeter fence on a Saturday night. No one knew about it until staff arrived on Monday.
ask: Which of the following explains why the fence did not reveal the break-in?
options: A fence detects only people who climb it
A fence works only when it is opaque
A fence delays entry but detects nothing
A fence protects only against vehicles
why: A plain fence detects no one, whether they climb it or cut it.
Opaque or transparent changes what can be seen, not whether a breach is reported.
A fence is a barrier; finding a breach needs cameras, sensors or patrols.
Fences are built to keep people out; stopping vehicles is mainly the job of bollards.

stem: The security lead at a water treatment plant needs a perimeter barrier that keeps people out. Guards in the watch tower must still see anyone approaching from outside the barrier.
ask: Which of the following BEST meets both needs?
why: A tall transparent fence keeps people out and lets the guards see through it.
A wall keeps people out, but guards cannot see through it.
Bollards leave gaps that people on foot walk through.
A painted line marks a boundary but keeps no one out.

stem: A physical security consultant hands the facilities manager of a research campus the perimeter specification below.
ask: Which of the following does line P-1 describe?

lines: P-1  3 m welded mesh, anti-climb, topped with barbed tape
P-2  Floodlights on the inside face every 25 m
P-3  Cameras covering the full boundary line
P-4  Two gates, each with a badge reader

why: Lighting is line P-2, the floodlights.
Video surveillance is line P-3, the cameras.
Badges are used at the gate readers in line P-4.
Welded anti-climb mesh with barbed tape along the boundary is a fence.

stem: A security architect at a corporate campus plans that every visitor must arrive through one staffed gate. Along the rest of the boundary, no one should be able to walk in.
ask: Which of the following does the boundary fence do in this plan, besides keeping people out?
options: Records who passes through the gate
Funnels all arrivals to one checkpoint
Stops vehicles at the lobby doors
why: A fence records nothing; cameras or badge logs would.
With the rest of the boundary closed, the fence channels everyone to the gate where they are checked.
Identity checks are done by the guard at the gate, not by the fence.
Stopping vehicles at a building front is the job of bollards.

stem: The site lead of a wind turbine parts depot learns that the far side of the depot's mesh fence cannot be seen from the office or the gate. She wants any crossing of that stretch to be noticed.
ask: Which of the following meet this need? (Select TWO)
options: Opaque panels in place of mesh
why: Cameras watching the line record a crossing and can alert on it, which the fence itself cannot do.
Razor wire makes the fence harder to climb, but it reports nothing.
Sensors raise an alert when someone crosses or disturbs the line.
Opaque panels hide the site from outside, but they detect no one.
Extra height adds delay, not detection.

ask: Which of the following is commonly used to authenticate a device on a corporate network?
options: A host name in a network list
A certificate from the company CA
A serial number on the device label
why: A host name is just a label any device can claim; it proves nothing.
A device certificate signed by the organization's CA proves the device is a trusted one.
A password authenticates the person, not the device.
A printed serial number can be read and copied; it is not proof.

ask: Which of the following questions does authenticating systems answer?
options: Is this user who they claim?
Is this device one of ours?
why: That is authenticating people.
That is authorization.
That is accounting.
Authenticating systems verifies that a device is the trusted one it claims to be.

stem: A network engineer at a toll road operator sets the camera network switches to admit a roadside camera only after it presents a certificate signed by the operator's internal CA and proves it holds that certificate's private key.
ask: Which of the following does this setting perform?
why: A certificate from the internal CA, plus proof that the camera holds its private key, verifies the device itself.
No person signs in here; the camera is checked, not a user.
Authorization decides what a proven identity may do; this setting proves the camera is a trusted one.
Accounting records activity; this setting checks the camera when it connects.

stem: A security administrator at a cooperative bank must stop staff from reaching back-office apps from personal laptops, even when they enter a valid password and approve a phone prompt.
ask: Which of the following meets this requirement?
why: A stronger password still works from a personal laptop.
Another user factor proves the person, not which laptop is used.
Only company laptops hold a certificate from the organization's CA, so personal laptops fail the check.
Logs record activity but do not block a personal laptop.

stem: A wireless administrator at a university must admit only university-owned tablets to the staff network. The network must also reject any tablet that copies an owned tablet's hardware address.
ask: Which of the following BEST meets these requirements?
why: It admits listed tablets, but a MAC address can be copied, which the stem says must be rejected.
Anyone given the passphrase can join from any device.
A captive portal collects a login or agreement; it does not prove the device is owned.
A copied hardware address does not give a device the certificate's private key, so only owned tablets pass.

stem: A PKI engineer at an aerospace supplier is asked why each device must sign a challenge when it connects, instead of only sending its certificate.
ask: Which of the following explains the challenge step?
options: It encrypts the certificate for transit
It proves possession of the private key
It renews the certificate before expiry
It hides the device's host name
why: Certificates are public; the step is about proof, not secrecy.
A certificate can be copied; signing a challenge shows the device has the matching private key.
Renewal is a separate process; the challenge happens at every connection.
The challenge does not hide any name; it proves key possession.

stem: A network team at a hospital requires both a device certificate and the nurse's MFA before anyone reaches the charting app.
ask: Which of the following does the device certificate add that the nurse's MFA does not?
options: Proof of who the user is
A record of what was opened
Proof the hardware holds an issued credential
why: The nurse's MFA already proves the person.
Recording activity is accounting, not part of device authentication.
The certificate, signed by the hospital's CA, shows the device holds a credential the hospital issued; the nurse's MFA says nothing about the device.
Keeping stored records secret is confidentiality through encryption, not a device check.

stem: A web developer at an online pharmacy wants customers' browsers to confirm they reached the real checkout server and not an impostor.
ask: Which of the following provides this assurance?
options: A certificate from a trusted CA
A hash shown on the checkout page
why: The browser checks that the server's certificate chains to a trusted CA, proving the server's identity.
A password proves the customer, not the server.
An impostor could show any hash; it does not prove the server's identity.
An address is an identifier, not proof; it can be spoofed or redirected.

stem: A systems engineer at a grocery chain inspects a point-of-sale terminal and finds the details below.
ask: Which of the following is this item used for?

lines: Private key: non-exportable, stored in TPM

options: Proving which cashier is signing in
why: A client certificate from the retailer's device CA lets the network verify which device is connecting; it does not show the terminal is patched or compliant.
The certificate names the device, not a person.
The usage is client authentication, not encrypting stored data.
Deciding rights is authorization, not what a device certificate does.

ask: Which of the following are accurate about device certificates? (Select TWO)
options: A copied certificate alone is enough to connect
They are signed by a CA the network trusts
They remove the need for user authentication
The device must prove it holds the private key
A MAC address serves the same purpose
why: Without the private key, a copied certificate fails the challenge.
The network accepts devices whose certificate chains to the trusted CA.
Device and user authentication answer different questions; many networks require both.
A copied certificate without its private key proves nothing.
A MAC address is an identifier that can be copied, not proof.

ask: Which of the following defines a microwave sensor?
options: A sensor that sends sound and reads the echoes
A sensor that receives heat and sends nothing
A sensor that reacts to weight on a mat
A sensor that sends radio pulses and reads reflections
why: Sound echoes are how an ultrasonic sensor works.
Receiving heat and sending nothing is how a passive infrared sensor works.
Weight on a mat is what a pressure sensor detects.
A microwave sensor sends out microwave pulses and detects movement from changes in what reflects back.

ask: Which of the following materials stops a microwave sensor's signal?
why: Microwaves pass through glass, which is a cause of false alarms.
Microwaves do not pass through metal.
Microwaves pass through drywall and can pick up movement in the next room.
Microwaves pass through wood.

stem: The facilities manager of an aircraft maintenance firm wants an alarm whenever anyone moves across any part of a large, open hangar floor at night.
ask: Which of the following should the manager install?
why: A pressure mat reports weight only at the spot where it lies, not movement across the whole floor.
A microwave sensor detects movement from changes in its reflected signal and is used to cover large open floor areas.
A door contact reports only that a door opened, not movement out on the floor.
A badge opens doors; it detects no movement on the floor.

stem: The office manager of an insurance broker gets night alarms from the motion sensor in the records room. The alarms happen when cleaners work in the next room, behind a drywall partition.
ask: Which of the following sensor types behaves this way?
why: A pressure mat reacts only to weight on itself, not to people in another room.
Infrared senses heat in its own view and does not sense through walls.
Ultrasonic sound stays in the room and does not pass through the partition.
Microwaves pass through drywall, so movement in the next room can set it off.

stem: A sales rep for an alarm supplier explains that one of her motion sensors works with radio waves, while another works with sound beyond human hearing. A store owner asks for the radio-wave model.
ask: Which sensor does the store owner want?
why: The microwave sensor uses radio waves (microwaves).
The ultrasonic sensor is the sound-based model.
A passive infrared sensor senses heat and sends out no waves.
A pressure sensor reacts to weight and sends out no waves.

stem: The manager of a stationery wholesaler finds that the microwave motion unit in the paper store raises an alarm whenever the large metal ceiling fan is left running at night. No one is in the room.
ask: Which of the following explains these false alarms?
options: The fan's warm air looks like body heat
The fan's weight presses on a floor mat
The spinning blades reflect the signal
The fan's light switches the unit on
why: Sensing heat is how infrared works; a microwave unit ignores heat.
A ceiling fan puts no weight on the floor.
Metal reflects microwaves strongly, and moving blades change the reflection the sensor watches.
A microwave unit does not react to light.

stem: The security lead of a cold storage company must watch three small packing bays with one motion sensor mounted in the middle bay. The bays are divided by thin wooden partitions, and movement in all three must be detected.
ask: Which of the following sensors meets this need?
why: Infrared does not sense through wood, so it would watch only the middle bay.
A pressure mat reports weight at one spot, not movement in three bays.
Ultrasonic sound does not pass through the wooden partitions, so the outer bays stay unwatched.
Microwave energy passes through wood, so one unit can sense movement behind the partitions.

stem: An alarm installer leaves the service note below for the office manager of an engineering consultancy.
ask: Which problem were these changes made to fix?

lines: MW-2: range reduced from 30 m to 18 m
MW-2: re-aimed away from the glass office front
Next visit: confirm no alerts from street movement

options: Missed alarms in a dark storeroom
Alarms caused by heat from radiators
Alarms from motion beyond the room
A cut cable on a floor mat
why: Nothing in the note is about darkness or missed detections.
Heat sets off infrared units; MW-2 is a microwave unit.
Shorter range and aiming away from glass keep the microwave unit from sensing beyond the room.
A cut mat cable is a tamper alarm on a pressure sensor, not a range problem.

stem: During a walk test at a tire distributor, the alarm installer walks behind a row of tall steel racks, and the microwave motion unit at the front of the bay never triggers. Walking in the open aisles triggers it every time.
ask: Which of the following explains the missed detection?
options: Steel hides the installer's body heat
Steel absorbs the unit's high-pitched sound
Steel stops the unit sensing floor weight
Steel blocks the unit's radio signal
why: Body heat is what an infrared sensor reads; a microwave unit reads reflected radio energy.
Sound echoes are how an ultrasonic sensor works; a microwave unit sends out radio energy.
Weight on a surface is what a pressure sensor reads; a microwave unit senses motion through the air.
Microwave energy passes through glass, wood and drywall but not metal, so the racks leave a blind area behind them.

stem: The loss prevention lead of a retail chain compares motion sensors for the large open sales floor of a garden center.
ask: Which of the following statements about microwave sensors are accurate? (Select TWO)
options: They can sense through metal panels
They send out nothing of their own
They react only to body heat
They detect motion from reflected signals
They can sense through glass and drywall
why: Metal stops microwaves.
Microwave sensors are active; it is passive infrared that sends nothing.
Body heat is what infrared senses; microwave reads reflected signals.
Movement changes the microwave signal that bounces back, and the sensor reads that change.
Microwaves pass through glass, drywall and wood.

ask: Which of the following Zero Trust components makes the access decision itself?
why: The Policy Administrator carries out the decision; it does not make it.
The Policy Engine grants, denies or revokes access by evaluating the request.
Adaptive identity is a concept that adjusts verification, not the deciding component.
Threat scope reduction is a design goal, not a component.

ask: Which of the following inputs does the Policy Engine weigh besides the access policy?
why: Network location alone is not enough; the engine weighs many inputs.
Uptime is an availability measure, not an input to an access decision.
A handbook is a document for people, not an input the engine evaluates.
The Policy Engine combines policy with signals such as threat intelligence and identity data.

stem: A field technician at a telecom requests the outage map from a tablet. The request is refused because the tablet is missing required patches.
ask: Which of the following components made the refusal decision?
why: Deciding to deny because the device fails its patch check is the Policy Engine's job.
The Policy Administrator would carry out the denial, not decide it.
That is the rule framework the decision follows, not the component that decides.
Adaptive identity adjusts how much verification is asked; the stem describes a decision.

stem: An auditor at a credit union wants a record of every grant and deny decision on the lending app and the reason for each.
ask: Which of the following components logs each decision?
why: The Policy Administrator acts on decisions; the decision log is kept by the Policy Engine, which makes them.
Adaptive identity is a concept, not a component that keeps decision logs.
The Policy Engine also logs each decision it makes.
A gap analysis is a planning study, not a source of per-request decision logs.

stem: Partway through a session at a medical clinic, a threat feed flags the address a billing clerk is connecting from, and the clerk's access is withdrawn.
ask: Which of the following components decided to revoke the access?
why: The Policy Administrator carries out the revocation but does not decide it.
The enforcement point drops the connection when told; it does not decide.
The clerk and device are the requester, not the decision maker.
The Policy Engine can revoke access when new information arrives, such as a threat feed alert.

stem: A trainee at a bank tells the security team that the Policy Enforcement Point decides whether each session is allowed.
ask: Which of the following corrects the trainee?
options: The PEP decides and also enforces
The Policy Engine decides; the PEP enforces
The Policy Administrator decides; the PEP logs
The subject decides; the PEP relays
why: That repeats the mistake: the enforcement point never decides.
Deciding is the Policy Engine's job; the enforcement point only applies the decision.
The Policy Administrator acts on decisions; it does not make them.
The subject requests access; it cannot decide its own access.

stem: An identity analyst at a wine distributor must connect the HR system to the Zero Trust platform. Once HR marks someone as departed, that person's next request to any app must be refused.
ask: Which of the following components must receive the HR data?
why: The Policy Administrator carries out decisions and sets up sessions; it does not weigh identity data.
The PEP allows or blocks traffic as instructed; it never weighs identity data or decides.
The Policy Engine weighs identity data such as HR records with policy on each request, so it must receive the feed.
The implicit trust zone is the area behind the PEP; it takes no inputs and makes no decisions.

stem: A security analyst at an e-commerce company sees that a request was granted after the device posture, the user's role and a clean threat feed result were combined into one trust score.
ask: Which of the following components produced the trust score?
why: Combining policy, identity, device and threat data into a verdict is the Policy Engine's work.
The Policy Administrator acts on the verdict; it does not compute it.
The enforcement point applies the result in the traffic path.
The requester and its device are evaluated; they do not score themselves.

stem: A security engineer at a hotel group reads the log lines below.
ask: Which of the following components made the decision recorded here?
why: A decision reached from policy, posture and threat inputs is made by the Policy Engine.
The Policy Administrator carries out a GRANT; it does not reach it.
The enforcement point opens the path once told; it does not decide.
adiaz and LT-7731 are the requester being judged.

ask: Which of the following are accurate about the Policy Engine? (Select TWO)
options: It grants, denies or revokes access
It sits in the traffic path
It sits in the control plane
It issues session tokens to clients
It only reads the user's password
why: The Policy Engine is the decision maker.
That is the enforcement point.
Decisions are made in the control plane.
Issuing tokens is the Policy Administrator's job.
It weighs many inputs, including device posture and threat intelligence.

ask: Which of the following describes the role of the Zero Trust control plane?
options: Carries traffic between users and apps
Holds the devices that request access
Makes access decisions and manages policy
Stores backup copies of protected data
why: Carrying traffic is the data plane's job.
Requesting devices are on the data plane side.
The control plane defines policy, evaluates requests and configures enforcement.
Backups serve availability; they are not part of either Zero Trust plane.

source.chapter: Zero Trust control plane vs data plane

ask: Which of the following pairs of components belongs to the control plane?
why: The requester and its device are on the data plane.
Gateways in the traffic path enforce decisions on the data plane.
These carry traffic; they are not Zero Trust decision components.
Both are control plane components: one decides and one acts on the decision.

source.chapter: Zero Trust control plane vs data plane

stem: A temporary nurse at a clinic requests the lab results app. A central service weighs her identity against policy, decides, and then instructs the gateway what to do.
ask: Which of the following parts of the architecture holds the central service?
why: The data plane carries traffic and enforces; it does not decide.
Deciding on the request and configuring the gateway are control plane work.
That is the area behind an enforcement point, not where decisions are made.
Zero Trust does not place decisions in a perimeter network.

source.chapter: Zero Trust control plane vs data plane

stem: A Zero Trust design team at a bank lists adaptive identity, threat scope reduction and policy-driven access control together under one plane.
ask: Which of the following explains why these belong in the control plane?
options: They are paths that carry traffic
They are the devices making requests
They are ways of making decisions
They are areas trusted after a gateway
why: Carrying traffic is the data plane's job.
Requesting devices are on the data plane side.
All three shape how access decisions are made, which is the control plane's job.
Areas behind a gateway are implicit trust zones on the data plane.

source.chapter: Zero Trust control plane vs data plane

stem: An identity engineer at a botanical garden edits one access rule in the central policy service. Within a minute, every gateway in front of the ticketing and membership apps begins applying the new rule.
ask: Which of the following describes how the rule reached the gateways?
options: The control plane configured each gateway
Each gateway wrote its own copy of the rule
Users' devices carried the rule to the gateways
The trust zone behind each gateway shared it
why: The control plane defines policy and configures the enforcement points that apply it.
Gateways are enforcement points in the data plane; they apply rules, they do not write them.
Requesting devices are subjects and systems in the data plane; they do not deliver policy.
An implicit trust zone is the area behind a gateway where resources sit; it does not hand out rules.

source.chapter: Zero Trust control plane vs data plane

stem: During a Zero Trust rollout at a shipping line, a gateway in front of the cargo app receives an instruction from the policy service to allow one session.
ask: Which of the following correctly places the two parts?
options: Gateway: data plane; service: control plane
Gateway: control plane; service: data plane
Both are in the control plane
Both are in the data plane
why: The gateway carries and enforces traffic; the policy service decides and instructs.
This reverses them: the service decides, so it is the control plane.
The gateway sits in the traffic path, which is the data plane.
The policy service decides, which is control plane work.

source.chapter: Zero Trust control plane vs data plane

stem: A router engineer at a regional internet provider notes that routers also have a control plane and a data plane, as Zero Trust does.
ask: Which of the following ideas do both uses of the terms share?
options: The data plane writes the policy
One part decides, the other forwards
The control plane stores user files
why: Only the data plane carries the traffic.
Policy and decisions belong to the control plane in both uses.
In routers and in Zero Trust, the control plane decides and the data plane carries traffic.
Neither plane is a file store; the control plane decides.

source.chapter: Zero Trust control plane vs data plane

stem: A security architect at a city government adds a new component that evaluates each access request and grants or denies it.
ask: Which of the following places this component correctly?
options: Data plane, as the enforcement point
Control plane, as the Policy Engine
Control plane, as the trust zone
why: The enforcement point applies decisions; it does not make them.
The component that grants or denies is the Policy Engine, in the control plane.
The subject is the requester, not the decision maker.
Trust zones are areas behind enforcement points on the data plane, not decision makers.

source.chapter: Zero Trust control plane vs data plane

stem: A solutions engineer at a glassworks reviews the module list of a Zero Trust product before deployment.
ask: Which of the following lists every module that belongs in the control plane?

lines: risk-scoring    rates each sign-in low, medium or high
rule-store      holds the central access rules
session-broker  issues tokens, tells gateways to open paths
edge-proxy      sits in front of each app, passes or blocks

why: edge-proxy is in the traffic path, a data plane enforcement point, and risk-scoring is left out.
This leaves out session-broker, which plays the Policy Administrator in the control plane.
edge-proxy is a data plane enforcement point, and risk-scoring and rule-store are left out.
Risk scoring, the central rules and the token and instruction service all decide or manage, so all three sit in the control plane.

source.chapter: Zero Trust control plane vs data plane

ask: Which of the following belong to the Zero Trust control plane? (Select TWO)
why: The enforcement point sits in the traffic path, on the data plane.
The requester and its device are on the data plane.
The zone behind an enforcement point is on the data plane.
The Policy Engine makes access decisions in the control plane.
The Policy Administrator acts on decisions from the control plane.

ask: Which of the following does the availability goal of the CIA triad protect?
options: Data stays secret from unauthorized parties
Authorized users can reach data when needed
Senders cannot deny sending their data
why: Keeping data secret is confidentiality, a different leg of the triad.
Keeping data accurate and unchanged is integrity, a different leg of the triad.
Availability keeps systems and data accessible to authorized users when they need them.
That is non-repudiation, a separate concept and not one of the three legs.

ask: Which of the following pairs a CIA triad goal with a control that protects it?
why: Hashing detects any change to data, which protects integrity.
Redundant servers keep a service running, which protects availability, not secrecy.
Encryption keeps data secret, which protects confidentiality, not access.
Fault tolerance keeps systems running through failures, which protects availability.

stem: A records manager at a county court must be able to detect whether anyone alters a stored judgment file, even an employee with valid permission to open it.
ask: Which of the following controls meets this requirement?
why: Fault tolerance keeps systems running through failures; it does not detect changes.
Redundant servers keep the file reachable; they do not detect changes.
Access controls limit who can open the file, but the stem includes employees who already have permission.
A stored hash no longer matches once the file changes, so any alteration is detected.

stem: A help desk lead at an online retailer must keep the order site running if one web server fails during a holiday sale.
ask: Which of the following controls supports this requirement?
why: Hashing detects changes to data; it does nothing when a server fails.
A second server takes over when one fails, which keeps the site available.
Encryption keeps data secret; it does not keep the site running.
Signatures prove data is unchanged and who signed it; they do not keep a service up.

stem: A pharmacist at a pharmacy chain finds that an intruder edited the dosage values in several stored prescriptions. No prescriptions were copied out, and the system stayed online.
ask: Which of the following security goals did the intruder harm?
why: Nothing was disclosed; the stem says no prescriptions were copied out.
Unauthorized changes to stored data harm integrity.
The system stayed online, so access was not lost.
No one is denying having sent or signed something; the harm is that records were changed.

stem: An HR manager at a staffing agency learns that a spreadsheet of employee salaries was emailed to an outside personal account. The file was not changed, and every system stayed up.
ask: Which of the following security goals was harmed?
why: The stem says the file was not changed.
Every system stayed up, so access was not lost.
Accounting is the AAA function that records what users did, not a goal of the triad; the harm here is that data was disclosed.
Salary data reached someone not authorized to see it, which harms confidentiality.

stem: A site reliability engineer at a concert ticket seller watches the event page time out for every buyer while hijacked devices around the world flood it with requests. No data was viewed or modified.
ask: Which of the following security goals did this attack target?
why: A flood that stops the site from answering is a DDoS attack on availability.
No data was read, so nothing was disclosed.
No data was altered.
No sender is denying an action; the site simply stopped answering.

stem: A practice manager at a dermatology clinic must send patient skin photos to an outside specialist over the internet. Anyone who captures the traffic on the way must be unable to view the photos.
ask: Which of the following controls meets this requirement?
why: A hash reveals changes to the photos, but anyone who captures them can still view them.
A signature proves who sent the photos and that they are unchanged, but it does not hide them.
Encryption makes captured photos unreadable without the key, which protects confidentiality.
Redundant links keep the connection up, which serves availability; captured photos stay viewable.

stem: A security analyst at a regional hospital reviews the incident queue below.
ask: Which of the following security goals did TKT-2052 harm?

lines: TKT-2041  Price table on the web shop changed by an unknown account
TKT-2047  Patient list posted on a public file share
TKT-2052  Ticketing system offline after its only disk failed
TKT-2058  Visitor log printed and left in the lobby

why: That fits TKT-2041, where data was changed; TKT-2052 changed nothing.
That fits TKT-2047 and TKT-2058, where data was exposed; TKT-2052 exposed nothing.
No one in TKT-2052 is denying an action; a system went offline.
TKT-2052 is a system that cannot be reached after a failure, which harms availability.

stem: A records officer at a land registry sends deed transfers to a county tax office each night. The tax office must be able to detect whether any deed was altered after the registry released it.
ask: Which of the following controls meet this requirement? (Select TWO)
why: Backup power keeps systems running, which serves availability; it detects no change.
A deed that no longer matches its hash value has been altered, so the change is detected.
Clustered servers keep the service reachable, which serves availability; they detect no change.
Fault tolerance keeps systems working through failures; it detects no change.
A registry signature fails to verify on any deed changed after it was signed, so the change is detected.

ask: Which of the following combinations is multifactor authentication?
options: Password plus a phone app code
why: A password is something you know and the phone is something you have: two different factor types.
Both are something you know, so this is still one factor type.
Two passwords are the same factor type, which is not MFA.
The username only identifies; the password is the single factor.

ask: Which of the following factor types is a fingerprint scan?
why: A fingerprint is a biometric trait of the person.
Knowledge factors are things remembered, such as a password.
Possession factors are objects held, such as a phone or token.
This refers to location, not a body trait.

stem: An office manager at a veterinary clinic signs in to the records system by typing a password and then pressing a finger on a reader.
ask: Which of the following describes this sign-in?
why: Two different factor types are used, so it is more than one factor.
Authorization decides what she may do after sign-in; the stem describes proving who she is.
A password (something you know) plus a fingerprint (something you are) are two different factor types.
Accounting records activity; the stem describes proving identity.

stem: An IT coordinator at a school district notices that the staff portal asks for a password and then for the name of the first school each person attended.
ask: Which of the following describes the portal's sign-in?
why: Two items of the same factor type are not MFA.
Both the password and the school name are something you know, so only one factor type is used.
Authorization decides rights after sign-in; the portal is proving identity.
Identification is only the username claim; the portal is asking for proof.

stem: A security engineer at a payment processor must add a second factor to administrator logins that already use a password.
ask: Which of the following would satisfy the requirement?
why: A longer password is still the same factor.
A question is something you know, the same type as the password.
A passphrase is something you know, the same type as the password.
A token is something you have, a different type from the password.

stem: An identity administrator at an architecture firm points out that staff usernames appear in every email signature the firm sends.
ask: Which of the following explains why a username alone cannot authenticate a user?
options: It is only a claim of identity
why: A username is not an object the user holds.
A username is not a body trait.
A username identifies the user; it is public, so it proves nothing.
Deciding rights is authorization; a username does neither.

stem: A plant manager at a chemical maker wants floor supervisors to sign in at control stations with a smart card and a fingerprint.
ask: Which of the following factor types does this combine?
options: Something you have and something you are
Something you know and something you are
Something you have and something you know
Two instances of something you have
why: A smart card is held (have) and a fingerprint is a trait (are).
No password or other remembered item is used.
A fingerprint is a trait, not something remembered.
A fingerprint is not an object held.

stem: A phishing email gave an outsider the password of a sales representative at a car dealership. The sales system also requires a code from an app on the representative's registered phone.
ask: Which of the following stops the outsider from signing in?
options: The length of the stolen password
why: The outsider already holds the password, so its length no longer helps.
Encryption hides traffic in transit; it does not stop someone holding a valid password.
Accounting records the attempt; it does not block it.
Without the registered phone, the outsider cannot supply the second factor.

stem: A facilities security engineer at a colocation provider reviews the settings below for the reader on a customer cage door.
ask: Which of the following describes the authentication these settings enforce?
why: Both steps are something you are, one factor type, so this is not MFA.
Both steps are biometrics, so only one factor type, something you are, is checked.
Authorization decides what a proven identity may do; these steps only prove identity.
Accounting records what was done; these steps check who is at the door.

ask: Which of the following pairs count as multifactor authentication? (Select TWO)
why: A card (have) and a passcode (know) are two different types.
Both are something you know.
A fingerprint (are) and a token (have) are two different types.
Both are something you know.
Both are something you have.

ask: What is a honeypot?
options: A network of several linked decoy systems
A single decoy system made to look like a real target
A live server that runs real business services
A filter that blocks attackers at the network edge
why: Several linked decoys form a honeynet, not a single honeypot.
A honeypot is a decoy, usually one whole system, that looks valuable and is built to attract and study attackers.
A honeypot has no real users or business services; any contact with it is suspect.
A honeypot detects and diverts attackers; it does not block attacks on real systems.

ask: Which of the following does a honeypot normally hold?
options: A live copy of production data
Fake data that only looks valuable
why: Real data on a decoy would put it at risk; a honeypot holds none.
Real customer records never belong on a decoy.
A honeypot looks like a valuable target but holds no real data.
Backups are real data and belong on protected systems, not a decoy.

stem: A network engineer at a regional bank sets up one fake server that looks like an old payment gateway. It holds no real data, and every connection to it is recorded.
ask: Which of the following is the engineer's goal?
options: Serving real customers at busy times
Keeping a spare copy of the gateway
why: It holds no real data and serves no customers.
A spare copy would hold real data; this server is fake.
A decoy records attackers; it does not block them.
A decoy that records every connection lets the team watch what attackers do.

stem: A security analyst at a logistics firm has run one decoy server for a year. The CISO (chief information security officer) now wants several decoy servers, workstations and a router linked to look like a branch office.
ask: Which of the following has the analyst been running for the past year?
why: A honeynet is what the CISO now wants: many linked decoys.
The analyst runs a server, not a file.
One decoy server on its own is a honeypot.
The analyst runs a server, not a planted credential.

stem: A penetration tester hired by a pharmacy chain finds a server named "trap-01" that runs default settings and carries no traffic at all. She ignores it and moves on.
ask: Which honeypot weakness does this show?
options: A poorly built decoy can be spotted
A decoy blocks testers from real servers
A decoy exposes real customer records
A decoy can only sit outside the network
why: An obvious name, default settings and no traffic gave the decoy away.
Nothing was blocked; the tester simply skipped the decoy.
The decoy holds no real records.
Decoys can sit inside the network; placement is not the problem here.

stem: A junior administrator at a game publisher plans to put a honeypot on the same flat network as the production database, with open routes between them.
ask: Which of the following is the main risk of this placement?
options: The honeypot would raise too few alerts
Every login would need legal approval
The decoy would slow database queries
An attacker could use it to reach real systems
why: Placement next to production does not reduce the decoy's alerts.
Legal review may be needed for a honeypot, but not for each login, and it is not the risk of this placement.
A separate decoy does not slow the real database.
Without isolation, an attacker who takes over the decoy can launch attacks on production.

stem: The security lead of a city government wants to know whether attackers inside the network are scanning servers and trying to log in to them. The budget covers only one decoy system, physical or virtual.
ask: Which of the following should the security lead deploy?
why: A honeynet needs several decoy systems, even when they run as virtual machines, more than the budget covers.
One decoy system alerts on any scan or login attempt against it.
A decoy file shows folder browsing, not scans and logins against servers.
A honeytoken shows fake data being used, not servers being scanned.

source.chapter: Honeypot vs honeynet vs honeyfile vs honeytoken (deception technologies compared)

stem: A security analyst at a frozen food maker reads the entries below from a decoy database server.
ask: Which of the following can the team learn from these entries?
options: Which real database the attacker breached
The attacker's address and the tool brought in
Where stolen data was later offered for sale
Which shared folder the attacker opened
why: trap-sql01 is a decoy; no real database appears.
The decoy recorded where the connection came from and the program uploaded.
Tracing data after it leaves is what honeytokens do.
Folder access is what a honeyfile reports; no folder appears here.

stem: A threat researcher at a university places a honeypot so that it faces the internet directly.
ask: Which of the following will this placement mainly show?
why: Lateral movement is caught by decoys inside the network, ideally a honeynet.
Folder browsing is shown by honeyfiles on internal shares.
Use of stolen data is shown by honeytokens.
An internet-facing decoy collects scans and attacks from outside.

stem: The IT director of a cosmetics company asks the security team what a planned honeypot will and will not do.
ask: Which of the following statements about the honeypot are accurate? (Select TWO)
options: It must be isolated from real systems
It blocks attacks on production servers
It shows where stolen files end up
It gives alerts with very few false positives
why: Isolation stops a captured decoy from attacking production.
A honeypot holds only fake data.
It detects and diverts; it does not block attacks elsewhere.
Tracing where data ends up is what honeytokens do.
Normal traffic never goes to a decoy, so its alerts are high confidence.

ask: Which of the following describes a security gap analysis?
options: Comparing current controls with a target standard
Testing whether attacks against systems succeed
Scanning hosts for known software flaws
Recording who signed in and when
why: A gap analysis compares the current posture with a desired state to find what is missing.
Trying attacks is penetration testing, which does not measure against a standard.
Finding technical flaws on hosts is a vulnerability scan, not a program-wide comparison.
Recording sign-ins is accounting.

ask: What does a gap analysis usually produce?
options: A list of hosts that were broken into
A prioritized plan to close the gaps
A log of each user's sessions
why: Formal certification comes from an audit; a gap analysis prepares for one.
That would come from a penetration test.
The result is a roadmap that ranks the gaps and plans how to close them.
Session logs are accounting records.

stem: A compliance manager at a robotics maker lists each requirement in an industry standard, notes which ones the company already meets, and marks the rest for a project plan.
ask: Which of the following describes the manager's work?
options: Testing whether attackers can break in
Reviewing logs for signs of misuse
Measuring the distance from a target baseline
why: Nothing is being attacked; requirements are being compared.
No hosts are being scanned; the manager is comparing practices with a standard.
Log review looks at past activity, not at how the program compares with a standard.
Comparing what is met against the standard's requirements, then planning the rest, is a gap analysis.

stem: After comparing its controls with ISO/IEC 27001, a security manager at a regional airport colors each area of the result green, yellow or red.
ask: Which of the following explains why the areas are colored?
options: So auditors can sign a certificate
So the biggest gaps are fixed first
So attackers cannot read the report
So each area gets the same budget
why: Color scores rank gaps for planning; they are not a certification.
Scoring each area shows which gaps are worst, so they can be handled first.
Colors do not protect the report; they rank the findings.
The point of ranking is to spend first where the gaps are biggest, not equally.

stem: The security director at a card payment processor wants to know how far the whole security program is from the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, covering policies, staff training and technology.
ask: Which of the following BEST meets this need?
why: A scan finds technical flaws on hosts, but it says nothing about policies or training.
Trying attacks examines part of the technology, but it does not measure policies or training against a framework.
Comparing the whole program against a framework, people and process included, is a gap analysis.
A tabletop exercise rehearses incident response; it does not compare the program with a framework.

stem: A newly hired security manager at a cruise line is asked to run the company's first gap analysis.
ask: Which of the following should the manager do FIRST?
options: Choose the framework to measure against
Buy tools for the largest gaps
Rate each gap red, yellow or green
Write the action plan with owners
why: Without a target baseline there is nothing to measure a gap against.
The gaps are not known yet; buying first skips the comparison.
Gaps can be rated only after the comparison finds them.
The action plan comes last, after the gaps are found and ranked.

stem: Months before an independent external audit, a compliance lead at a medical laboratory compares current practices with the standard so the weaknesses can be fixed in time.
ask: Which of the following is the compliance lead carrying out?
why: An internal comparison against the standard to find and fix weaknesses ahead of an audit is a gap analysis.
The external audit is the later, independent check; the lead is preparing for it.
No attacks are being tried; practices are being compared with a standard.
No hosts are being scanned for flaws.

stem: A risk analyst at a hotel group rates each likely threat to the reservation system by how likely it is and how much harm it would cause.
ask: Which of the following activities is this?
why: A gap analysis measures distance from a target standard; it does not rate threats by likelihood and impact.
A scan finds flaws on hosts; it does not rate threats by likelihood.
Rating threats by likelihood and impact is a risk assessment.
A penetration test tries attacks; it does not score threats.

stem: A risk manager at a grain cooperative receives the gap analysis summary below.
ask: Which of the following gaps should the action plan address FIRST?

lines: G-01  Laptop encryption     62% of laptops encrypted    Yellow
G-02  Phishing drill        none held in two years      Red
G-03  Offsite backups       weekly and tested           Green
G-04  Visitor log review    monthly, as required        Green

why: Laptop encryption is a real gap, but rated Yellow, smaller than the Red one.
The phishing drill is the only area rated Red, the biggest gap.
Offsite backups are rated Green: the requirement is already met.
Visitor log review is rated Green: the requirement is already met.

ask: Which of the following are accurate about a gap analysis? (Select TWO)
options: It is often measured against a framework
It proves that attacks would fail
It is a scan of hosts for flaws
It can take weeks or months
why: Frameworks such as NIST or ISO/IEC 27001 are common targets.
It compares controls with a target; it does not test attacks.
It often prepares for an audit, but it is not the formal check.
That is a vulnerability scan.
A full analysis of a program takes time.
